days.title: Spark ML: When to Use It, Pipelines, Estimators and Transformers

concepts.heading: When Spark ML Is the Right Tool
concepts.body: Databricks recommends training on a single machine when possible, because distributed code is more complex than single-machine code and slower from communication overhead. Consider distributed training when the data or the model is too large to fit in memory on one machine. Single-node libraries such as scikit-learn are not distributed, so they run on the driver and extra workers do not speed them up. Spark ML, the DataFrame-based pyspark.ml API, runs each algorithm as Spark jobs: rows stay in partitions on the workers and every pass combines partial results, so memory and compute grow with the cluster, and scoring can run where the data already lives. Choose Spark ML when the training set will not fit on one node, the algorithm exists in pyspark.ml and is accurate enough, and scoring also runs on Spark. Keep scikit-learn on one node when the table is small or the single-node model already wins: prepare features in Spark and read them with toPandas(). A flat learning curve also allows training on a representative sample (general practice). In Spark one task processes one partition, so a table in 8 partitions keeps only 8 cores busy.

concepts.heading: Estimators, Transformers and Pipelines
concepts.body: A Transformer implements transform(), which turns one DataFrame into another, usually by appending columns; feature transformers and fitted models are both Transformers. An Estimator implements fit(), which takes a DataFrame and produces a Model, and that Model is a Transformer. A Pipeline chains stages, each a Transformer or an Estimator, and runs them in order. A Pipeline is itself an Estimator: fit() returns a PipelineModel in which every Estimator has become a fitted Transformer. At scoring time the PipelineModel sends new data through the same learned processing, which is the main reason to put every step in the pipeline instead of preparing columns by hand. Because a Pipeline is an Estimator, one featurization Pipeline can be the first stage of several model pipelines, and a CrossValidator can tune the whole pipeline so preprocessing is refitted on each training fold. Stages must be unique instances, and a Pipeline checks types at run time against the DataFrame schema, not at compile time, so a missing or mistyped column fails only when the pipeline runs.

concepts.heading: Stages That Learn and Stages That Only Apply
concepts.body: Pick the stage by asking whether it must learn from training data. Estimators learn state that the fitted model keeps: StringIndexer maps strings to indices (frequencyDesc by default, so index 0 is the most frequent value) and IndexToString turns predictions back into labels; Imputer fills missing numeric values with the mean, median or mode; QuantileDiscretizer learns quantile splits and returns a Bucketizer, and may use fewer buckets than requested when there are few distinct values; StandardScaler and MaxAbsScaler learn column statistics. Row-level logic needs no learning: SQLTransformer runs a SELECT over __THIS__, so a derived column such as clicks / impressions becomes a saved pipeline stage. Two scaler details matter. StandardScaler has withMean false by default because centering builds a dense output, which is risky for sparse input, while MaxAbsScaler divides by the largest absolute value and keeps sparsity. KMeans uses distances, so scale features first or the widest range decides the clusters. Indices belong to the model that learned them: store raw categories in shared tables, not indexed values.

concepts.heading: Text, Vector and Streaming Stages
concepts.body: HashingTF is a Transformer that hashes terms into numFeatures buckets with MurmurHash 3. It needs no global dictionary, which suits a huge corpus, but different terms can collide and the mapping from position back to word is not kept. CountVectorizer is an Estimator that builds a vocabulary, limited by vocabSize and document-frequency thresholds such as minDF, and its model stores that vocabulary, so choose it when reviewers need the top words behind coefficients. VectorAssembler combines columns into one vector column and needs the size of every input vector. For a batch DataFrame Spark can inspect the data; in a streaming DataFrame the contents are not available until the stream starts, so place a VectorSizeHint(inputCol, size) stage before the assembler to put the size into the column metadata. The handleInvalid option of VectorSizeHint is error by default, with skip to drop bad rows and optimistic to skip the check. Missing values are another frequent failure: VectorAssembler rejects nulls by default, so impute inside the pipeline instead of dropping rows, which changes the population.

examPoints: Distributed training pays communication overhead: keep one node when the data and model fit in memory, and choose Spark ML when the training set will not fit and scoring also runs on Spark.

A Pipeline is an Estimator whose fit returns a PipelineModel; learned state (Imputer, StringIndexer, QuantileDiscretizer, scalers) lives in the fitted model, and stateless row logic belongs in SQLTransformer.
Match the stage to the symptom: MaxAbsScaler for sparse vectors, scaling before KMeans, CountVectorizer when words must be recovered, VectorSizeHint for vectors in a streaming DataFrame.

quiz.q: A media company keeps 1.2 billion click events in a Delta table. After feature encoding, the training set is larger than the memory of the biggest node type available. A logistic regression must be retrained nightly on the full history, and scoring runs later on the same Spark cluster. Which training approach fits?
choices: Move to a single-node cluster with the largest driver type and fit scikit-learn LogisticRegression after calling toPandas() on the whole training DataFrame
Keep scikit-learn on the driver and set n_jobs=-1, so that the worker cores of the cluster share the work of a single fit
Fit a Spark ML Pipeline that ends in LogisticRegression on the DataFrame, so the rows stay partitioned
Train scikit-learn on a 0.1% random sample, since the rare customer segments in the data add little to the model
quiz.explain: The training set does not fit in the memory of any single node, so a single-node fit is impossible. Spark ML keeps rows in partitions on the workers and combines partial results, and the same pipeline scores on Spark. A scikit-learn fit runs on the driver however many workers exist, so n_jobs cannot use them, and a tiny sample throws away the rare segments the business needs.

quiz.q: A 200-million-row churn table has nulls in income and tenure_months. The VectorAssembler stage fails on them, and filtering the null rows removes new customers. Scoring must reuse exactly the fill values learned on the training data. What should the team do?
choices: Add an Imputer with the median strategy before the VectorAssembler, so the fitted pipeline stores the medians
Replace the nulls with zero using DataFrame.fillna in the training notebook and repeat the same call in the scoring job
Set VectorAssembler handleInvalid to skip, so that rows containing nulls are removed at fit time and at scoring time
Compute the column medians with a separate aggregation job and write them as constants into the SQLTransformer statement
quiz.explain: Imputer is an Estimator: fit learns one surrogate value per column and the resulting model keeps it, so the PipelineModel applies the same numbers at scoring. Zero is a wrong fill for income and must be repeated by hand, skipping rows drops the new customers again, and hard-coded constants go stale and are not saved with the model.

days.recap: Use Spark ML when the data will not fit one node and scoring runs on Spark, otherwise stay on one machine. Put every learned step into a Pipeline so the PipelineModel repeats it at scoring, use SQLTransformer for stateless logic, and choose scalers and text stages by how they treat sparsity, vocabularies and streaming vector sizes.

days.title: Tuning, Evaluating and Scoring Spark ML Models

concepts.heading: Tuning with CrossValidator and TrainValidationSplit
concepts.body: MLlib tuning needs three things: an Estimator or a whole Pipeline, a list of ParamMaps and an Evaluator. CrossValidator splits the data into folds, averages the metric over the folds for each ParamMap, then refits the Estimator with the best ParamMap on the entire dataset. With 3 values of one parameter, 2 of another and 2 folds it trains (3 x 2) x 2 = 12 models. TrainValidationSplit evaluates each ParamMap once on a single train and validation pair set by trainRatio; it is cheaper but less reliable on small data. By default ParamMaps are evaluated in serial. Setting parallelism to 2 or more fits that many models at once; the docs say to choose it without exceeding cluster resources, that larger values may not help, and that up to 10 is generally enough. Fits that already fill the cluster gain nothing. foldCol names an integer column from 0 to numFolds minus 1 and replaces random folds, so a hash of customer_id keeps all rows of one customer in the same fold. Random folds can leak groups and future rows; a time-based split suits forecasting (general practice).

concepts.heading: Choosing the Evaluator and Reading the Metric
concepts.body: The Evaluator decides which ParamMap wins, so match it to the task: RegressionEvaluator, BinaryClassificationEvaluator, MulticlassClassificationEvaluator, MultilabelClassificationEvaluator, RankingEvaluator, and ClusteringEvaluator for clustering. MulticlassClassificationEvaluator defaults to the f1 metric; for a rare class use a per-label metric such as recallByLabel together with metricLabel, whose default is 0. RankingEvaluator offers metrics such as ndcgAtK with k defaulting to 10, which judge a recommended list rather than a rating error. ClusteringEvaluator computes the silhouette from the features and prediction columns, so it needs no label and can pick k for KMeans. ALS returns NaN for users or items unseen in training, and an evaluator averaging NaN returns NaN; coldStartStrategy set to drop removes those rows so the metric is valid. A model summary describes the training set, so judge quality on a held-out split. The best average from CV is the maximum of many noisy estimates, so keep a test set that tuning never touches. A binary threshold defaults to 0.5; choose it on validation data against the business target.

concepts.heading: Batch and Streaming Scoring with a PipelineModel
concepts.body: A fitted PipelineModel scores with transform(), which is lazy and runs on the cluster. For a nightly batch, make the write idempotent: Delta mode overwrite with the replaceWhere option replaces only the rows that match a predicate, such as one score_date, so a retry cannot duplicate rows. Spark ML stores probabilities in a vector column that SQL users cannot index; vector_to_array turns it into an array of doubles. In practice fit() runs on a bounded dataset, since a streaming DataFrame only runs through writeStream, so for streaming fit once on a static table, save the PipelineModel, and call transform on the streaming DataFrame. A stream-static join to a feature table is not stateful, so it needs no state management. For incremental scoring without a cluster running all day, schedule a job with trigger(availableNow=True): it processes what is available when it starts, then stops, and a checkpoint remembers progress. A model loaded once at start-up is not refreshed when an alias later moves (general behavior), so restart the query or load the model per micro-batch.

concepts.heading: Spark ML or a Single-Node Model for Inference
concepts.body: Inference style decides the design, not the training tool. Batch over very large tables wants throughput: a Spark ML PipelineModel runs transform in the JVM next to the data, and a single-node model can still be scaled out with mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf, which the docs show for batch and streaming scoring on a Spark cluster. A few thousand rows fit one small node: load the model with mlflow.pyfunc.load_model and call predict on pandas, because starting executors costs more than the scoring. For deep models stored as files, pyspark.ml.functions.predict_batch_udf takes a make_predict_fn that loads the model and caches its predict function, so the load is not repeated for every batch. Streaming should score inside the query, with spark_udf or an iterator pandas UDF, not by collecting each micro-batch with toPandas() to the driver, where batch size is unbounded. Real-time requests of one row cannot pay Spark job start-up: register the model and create a Model Serving endpoint. With equal accuracy, a Spark ML pipeline typically avoids Python workers and matching Python packages.

examPoints: CrossValidator averages the metric over folds and refits the best ParamMap on all data; TrainValidationSplit evaluates once; parallelism helps only when fits do not already fill the cluster, and foldCol keeps groups together.

Match the evaluator to the task (recallByLabel with metricLabel for a rare class, RankingEvaluator for recommendation lists, ClusteringEvaluator for unlabeled KMeans) and report quality on a test set that tuning never saw.

Fit on static data and call transform on a stream; use replaceWhere for idempotent batch writes, availableNow for incremental scheduled scoring, spark_udf for batch scale-out and Model Serving for one-row real-time calls.

quiz.q: A fraud model is tuned with CrossValidator(numFolds=5). Each customer has many transactions, and cross-validation scores are far higher than the scores seen on new customers after deployment. Which change addresses the cause?
choices: Raise numFolds from 5 to 10 so that every fold holds fewer transactions from any customer
Add a fold column such as abs(hash(customer_id)) % 5 and pass it with setFoldCol
Replace CrossValidator by TrainValidationSplit with trainRatio 0.8, which evaluates each ParamMap once
Set parallelism to 10 so that the folds run at the same time and the random split is repeated several times
quiz.explain: Random folds spread one customer's rows across training and validation, so the model is scored on customers it has already seen. foldCol takes an integer from 0 to numFolds minus 1 and replaces the random split, so hashing the customer key keeps each customer in a single fold. More folds and a random single split still mix customers, and parallelism changes speed, not the split.

quiz.q: A streaming job reads events with spark.readStream and tries to run Pipeline([StringIndexer(...), VectorAssembler(...), LogisticRegression()]).fit on the streaming DataFrame. Spark rejects it. What is the correct design?
choices: Call fit inside foreachBatch on every micro-batch, so that the pipeline is refitted continuously on the newest events
Add a watermark to the streaming DataFrame before calling fit, so that the pipeline sees a bounded window of events
Convert the stream to pandas with toPandas() and fit a scikit-learn pipeline once for each micro-batch of events
Fit on a static training table once, save the PipelineModel, and call its transform on the streaming DataFrame
quiz.explain: fit makes several passes over the data and needs a bounded dataset, while a streaming DataFrame can only run through writeStream. A fitted PipelineModel only applies learned state, so transform works on a stream. Refitting per micro-batch changes the learned mapping and the model with every batch, a watermark does not make a stream finite, and toPandas() on a stream is not available.

days.recap: Tune whole pipelines with CrossValidator, use foldCol or a time split to stop leakage, and report the metric on an untouched test set. Match the evaluator to the task, fit pipelines on static data and transform on streams, and pick the inference path by volume and latency: Spark ML or spark_udf for batch, one small node for small tables, Model Serving for single rows.

days.title: Scaling Training with Spark ML and pandas Function APIs

concepts.heading: Keeping Spark ML Training Busy
concepts.body: Spark ML algorithms are ordinary Spark jobs, so one task processes one partition. If the training DataFrame has 8 partitions, at most 8 cores work on each pass, so compare the tasks in the Spark UI stage with the total executor cores and repartition to a small multiple of the core count, for example 320 for 10 workers with 16 cores (general Spark tuning practice). Iterative solvers such as logistic regression read the data once per iteration, and Spark evaluates DataFrames lazily. Without persistence, every pass re-runs the whole lineage of reads, joins and feature stages, so cache the assembled training DataFrame and run an action to materialize it before calling fit. When many small models train from the same features, fit them concurrently: the Spark job scheduling guide says that multiple parallel jobs can run inside one application if they are submitted from separate threads, and a fit is a set of jobs. Cache the shared features first. Prefer built-in column functions over Python UDFs, because they run in the JVM with no Python worker or serialization.

concepts.heading: pandas Function APIs and Their Limits
concepts.body: pandas function APIs apply a native Python function to pandas objects and use Apache Arrow to move data. There are three kinds. Grouped map, groupBy().applyInPandas(), is split-apply-combine: the function receives all rows of one group as a pandas DataFrame and returns a pandas DataFrame, and you supply a schema as a StructType or a string. Map, mapInPandas(), receives an iterator of pandas DataFrames and returns an iterator, so output can have any length. Cogrouped map, groupBy().cogroup().applyInPandas(), shuffles two DataFrames so groups with the same key meet, and the function receives two pandas DataFrames, which suits train and holdout pairs per key and as-of joins. Returned column labels must match the schema field names (or match by position when not named by strings). All data of a group or cogroup is loaded into memory first, so skewed groups can run out of memory, and maxRecordsPerBatch does not apply to groups. For plain pandas UDFs, Spark converts partitions to Arrow record batches, and lowering spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch (default 10,000) reduces memory use on wide rows.

concepts.heading: One Model per Group
concepts.body: Training a model per store, region or customer fits grouped map well: groupBy(key).applyInPandas(train_fn, schema) runs one call per group, groups run in parallel across the cluster, and each group can use any single-node library. Return something the schema can carry: the key, a metric and, in a binary column, the pickled model bytes (a common pattern, not a documented requirement), so a Delta table can hold both results and models. Parallelism equals the number of groups. With 12 regions only 12 tasks work, however large the cluster is. To tune per region, cross join the regions with a small table of candidate configurations and group by region and config id, so each pair is an independent task. Group size is bounded by one node, so very large groups need Spark ML instead. For inference per group or at scale, mapInPandas lets you load the model once before iterating over batches and yield a result for each batch, whereas a Series-to-Series pandas UDF repeats the load in its body for each batch. Returning metrics to the driver and logging them to MLflow from there is common practice.

examPoints: Spark ML parallelism follows partitions: repartition to a multiple of the cores, cache the training DataFrame for iterative solvers, and submit independent fits from separate threads.
applyInPandas gives one call per group with the whole group in memory; cogroup passes two DataFrames per key; mapInPandas passes an iterator of batches and returns any number of rows.
Per-group parallelism is capped by the number of groups and a group must fit one node; load models once before the loop in mapInPandas and a binary column is a common way to return model bytes.

quiz.q: A tuning job fits one model per region for 12 regions using groupBy('region').applyInPandas(fit_and_score, schema) on a cluster with 400 cores. Each candidate configuration is evaluated one after another inside the function, and most cores stay idle. Which redesign uses the cluster?
choices: Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to 400 so that the 12 regions are spread over all the available cores
Lower spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch so that each region is split into smaller Arrow batches
Replace applyInPandas with a Series-to-Series pandas UDF that receives the regions as separate columns
Cross join regions with the configurations and group by region and config id
quiz.explain: applyInPandas makes one call per group and sends all rows of a group to one task, so 12 groups keep at most 12 tasks busy whatever the shuffle partition count is. Making each region and configuration pair its own group creates many independent tasks. maxRecordsPerBatch does not apply to groups, and a pandas UDF over columns does not train per region.

quiz.q: A 1.5 GB scikit-learn model scores an 800-million-row table with a Series-to-Series pandas UDF that calls joblib.load in its body. Executors spend most of their time reading the model file. What change removes that cost?
choices: Use groupBy().applyInPandas() with the customer key, so that each group loads the model once
Use mapInPandas, load the model once before iterating over the batches and yield a result for each batch
Raise spark.sql.execution.arrow.maxRecordsPerBatch above the default, so that fewer batches call the function
Call toPandas() on the table and score it in a single loop on the driver where the model is loaded once
quiz.explain: The body of a Series-to-Series pandas UDF runs for every Arrow batch, so the model is loaded again each time. mapInPandas passes an iterator, and code before the loop runs once per task. Grouped map loads the file for every group, a bigger batch size risks memory errors on wide rows, and toPandas() collects 800 million rows on the driver.

days.recap: Make Spark ML use the whole cluster with enough partitions, cached training data and concurrent fits from separate threads. Use applyInPandas for one model per group, cogroup for paired data and mapInPandas for efficient inference, remembering that parallelism equals the number of groups and that a group must fit in memory.

days.title: Distributed Hyperparameter Tuning with Optuna and Ray

concepts.heading: Optuna Studies, Samplers and Pruners
concepts.body: Optuna is an open-source library for hyperparameter tuning that can scale horizontally. The search space is declared inside the objective function with trial.suggest_* calls, and the objective returns the value to optimize, for example a validation error. A range that spans many orders of magnitude needs log=True, as in trial.suggest_float('svr_c', 1e-10, 1e10, log=True), otherwise almost all samples land in the top decade. A Study is the record of finished trials. A sampler reads that record to choose the next parameters, and a pruner stops trials that look worse than earlier trials at the same step. The Databricks MlflowSparkStudy uses TPESampler as the default sampler and MedianPruner as the default pruner. Pruning needs intermediate values (Optuna behavior, not stated on the Databricks page), so the objective must report a value to the trial after each epoch or fold and stop when the trial is marked for pruning; a pruner cannot judge a trial that reports only at the end. Hyperopt with SparkTrials is a legacy path no longer maintained; its hp expressions outside the objective become suggest calls inside it.

concepts.heading: Distributing Optuna with MlflowSparkStudy
concepts.body: Databricks documents two classes added with MLflow 3.0. MlflowStorage lets Optuna use the MLflow tracking server, one experiment, as its storage backend, and it batches writes to avoid REST API throttling. MlflowSparkStudy wraps an Optuna Study to run parallel trials on PySpark executors. The pattern is: create MlflowStorage(experiment_id=...), create MlflowSparkStudy(study_name=..., storage=...), then call optimize(objective, n_trials=..., n_jobs=...) and read best_params. The storage must be shared, because with the default in-memory storage every worker keeps its own record, so 40 workers run 40 separate searches that never learn from each other. MLflow 3.0 is preinstalled in Databricks Runtime 17.1 ML and above; on older runtimes run %pip install mlflow --upgrade and %pip install optuna at the top of the notebook. If the import of MlflowSparkStudy fails, a runtime without MLflow 3 is the first thing to check. Each trial is tracked in the experiment, which gives a comparable history of parameters and values. The trial function is ordinary single-node training code, because the docs run trials on PySpark executors.

concepts.heading: Ray Tune on Databricks
concepts.body: Ray is an open-source framework for scaling Python applications, and Ray Tune provides scalable hyperparameter search. On Databricks, ray.util.spark.setup_ray_cluster starts a background Spark job in which each Spark task becomes a Ray worker node, and the Ray head node runs on the driver. Ray on Spark is supported on dedicated access mode, no isolation shared access mode and jobs clusters only; it cannot start on serverless compute. A cluster made in a notebook belongs to that user and shuts down when the notebook detaches or after 30 minutes without tasks. setup_global_ray_cluster, Ray 2.9.0 and above, makes a global mode cluster that every user on the compute can reach with ray.init(), with no inactivity timeout. Avoid %pip on a running Ray cluster because it shuts it down; install libraries first. For MLflow with Ray 2.41 and above, set DATABRICKS_HOST and a token, or a client ID and secret, as environment variables before setup_ray_cluster. Log from the driver, or give each task the parent run ID and start a child run. For hybrid GPU jobs set spark.task.resource.gpu.amount to 0, so Spark preprocessing leaves the GPUs to Ray.

concepts.heading: Choosing Between Optuna on Spark and Ray
concepts.body: Both tools run many independent trials. Use Optuna with MlflowSparkStudy when each trial is a single-node function, such as a scikit-learn or boosted-tree fit, you already run on a standard Databricks cluster, and you want the study and every trial recorded in one MLflow experiment with sampler and pruner choices. In general, use Ray Tune when trials are dynamic or GPU-heavy, when trials run for very different times and new work depends on earlier results, when analysts must share one long-lived cluster, or when the code already uses Ray Train. General practice for a shared budget: with a fixed number of GPUs, trial-level parallelism has almost no communication cost, whereas data parallelism inside a trial synchronizes at every step, so several trials on a few devices each often beat every trial on all devices in sequence. Neither tool replaces the choice of search algorithm: TPE and similar samplers learn from results, random search does not. Keep Hyperopt out of new designs because it is not maintained and is not in ML Runtime after 16.4 LTS.

examPoints: Distributed Optuna on Databricks needs shared storage: MlflowStorage on one experiment plus MlflowSparkStudy, which defaults to TPESampler and MedianPruner; MLflow 3.0 is preinstalled from Runtime 17.1 ML, otherwise install it with %pip.
Search spaces live inside the objective (suggest_float with log=True for wide ranges) and pruning works only if the objective reports intermediate values.

Ray on Spark needs dedicated, no isolation shared or jobs compute (not serverless), setup_global_ray_cluster shares one cluster, %pip stops a running cluster, and MLflow credentials must be set before setup_ray_cluster.

quiz.q: A team starts 40 parallel Optuna workers on Spark. Each worker builds its own study with the default in-memory storage, and the best value barely improves compared with 4 workers. How should the team fix the setup?
choices: Create the study on MlflowStorage and run it through MlflowSparkStudy, so all workers share one record
Give every worker a different random seed and merge the 40 best_params dictionaries by hand after the runs finish
Increase n_trials on each worker and keep the in-memory storage, so each worker explores a larger share of the space
Switch the sampler to RandomSampler on every worker, since a sampler that learns from trials needs more memory per trial
quiz.explain: With in-memory storage each worker keeps its own list of trials, so 40 independent searches run and no sampler sees the others' results. MlflowStorage uses the MLflow tracking server as shared storage, and MlflowSparkStudy runs the parallel trials on executors against it. Seeds, more trials and a random sampler leave the searches independent.

quiz.q: A data scientist runs a long Ray Tune search and then runs %pip install lightgbm in the same notebook. The search stops and the Ray cluster disappears. What is the documented practice?
choices: Use setup_global_ray_cluster, because a global mode cluster is not affected by library installation in a notebook
Attach the notebook to serverless compute, which keeps the Ray cluster alive while the Python environment restarts
Install the libraries before the Ray cluster is created, at the top of the notebook or as cluster libraries
Set DATABRICKS_HOST and a token as environment variables so that Ray reconnects after the package installation
quiz.explain: The Ray cluster is started from the notebook as a background Spark job, and running %pip on a running Ray cluster shuts it down. Libraries should be installed first, then setup_ray_cluster and ray.init. Serverless compute cannot host Ray on Spark, and credentials only matter for MLflow calls from tasks.

days.recap: Declare the Optuna search space in the objective, report intermediate values for pruning, and share one study across workers with MlflowStorage and MlflowSparkStudy. Choose Ray Tune for dynamic or GPU-heavy trials on a supported cluster, install libraries before creating the Ray cluster, and set MLflow credentials before setup_ray_cluster.

days.title: Scaling Strategy: Vertical vs Horizontal, Data vs Model Parallelism, Ray vs Spark

concepts.heading: Vertical or Horizontal Scaling
concepts.body: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine with more memory, cores or GPUs; horizontal scaling means more machines. Databricks advises training neural networks on a single machine when possible, because distributed training and inference code is more complex and slower due to communication overhead, and says to consider distribution when the model or the data cannot fit in memory on one machine. So scale up first: the code stays the same, debugging is easy, and a multi-GPU node avoids the network. Vertical scaling stops at the largest instance, and that node is a single point of failure, so plan to scale out when data keeps growing. Horizontal scaling adds memory and compute but pays synchronization costs, so returns diminish: a job on 8 nodes may speed up much less than 8 times because every step ends with an exchange between processes. As general practice, use the fewest machines that meet the time target. For classical algorithms, Databricks offers distributed Spark ML training through pyspark.ml.connect; from Databricks Runtime 17.0 Spark ML is enabled by default in Standard compute.

concepts.heading: Data Parallelism and Model Parallelism
concepts.body: Data parallelism keeps a full copy of the model in every process, divides the data into shards, and averages gradients between processes. Choose it when the model fits one device but the dataset or the number of steps is large. TorchDistributor launches PyTorch training as Spark jobs through torch.distributed.run; its arguments are num_processes, local_mode and use_gpu. Put imports such as import torch inside the training function to avoid pickling errors. With DistributedDataParallel, each process builds its own DataLoader, so pass a DistributedSampler or every process reads the full dataset. Use the nccl backend on GPUs and gloo on CPUs. The error ncclInternalError: Internal check failed means NCCL cannot use some network interfaces; the documented fix is os.environ['NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME'] = 'eth0' in the training code. Model parallelism splits the model across devices because one copy does not fit; replicating the full model is then impossible. The DeepSpeed distributor, built on TorchDistributor, is the recommended solution for models that need more compute but are limited by memory, with optimized memory use and pipeline parallelism.

concepts.heading: Ray and Spark Side by Side
concepts.body: Databricks describes Ray and Spark as complementary. Spark specializes in data parallelism: one operation over partitions of a large dataset, as in ETL, joins, aggregations and Spark ML. Ray excels at logical parallelism: many dynamic, compute-intensive tasks such as tuning, deep learning, reinforcement learning and per-item time series forecasting. Generally, Spark executes a planned set of stages, while Ray tasks can be launched dynamically as results arrive. Ray on Databricks keeps the platform benefits: Unity Catalog governance, MLflow tracking, Lakeflow Jobs, and Model Serving for models trained with Ray Train, so training with Ray does not mean leaving Databricks. A typical pipeline aggregates terabytes with Spark and then trains or tunes with Ray on the same cluster. Size the Ray cluster deliberately: setting num_cpus_worker_node to the CPU cores and num_gpus_worker_node to the GPUs of each Spark worker makes each worker launch one Ray worker using all its resources. The Ray head defaults to 0 CPUs and 0 GPUs. With a fixed node count, enable autoscaling so idle Ray workers free the nodes for Spark.

concepts.heading: A Decision Guide for Large-Scale Training
concepts.body: Work through the choice in order. First, does it fit one node? If yes, train there, using a larger or multi-GPU instance if needed, and keep Spark for feature preparation. Second, what is the algorithm? A classical algorithm that exists in pyspark.ml, such as logistic regression on a 2 TB Delta table, belongs in Spark ML, which is already a data-parallel job over a DataFrame. Third, for a deep-learning model that fits on one GPU but trains on huge data, use data parallelism with TorchDistributor or Ray Train. Fourth, if the weights and optimizer state do not fit one GPU, use DeepSpeed or another model-parallel approach. Fifth, for thousands of independent, uneven, stateful or dynamically created tasks, use Ray. Finally, split a fixed GPU budget: running several trials, each on a few devices, usually beats running each trial across all devices one after another, because independent trials need no communication. A single-node library does not distribute by itself: n_jobs uses the driver cores only.

examPoints: Start with one machine and scale up; distribute only when data or model exceed memory, and expect diminishing returns from synchronization when adding nodes.
Data parallelism copies the model per process (TorchDistributor with a DistributedSampler); when one copy does not fit, use the DeepSpeed distributor; NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME fixes ncclInternalError.
Spark is data parallelism for ETL and Spark ML, Ray is logical parallelism for dynamic compute tasks; set num_cpus_worker_node and num_gpus_worker_node to the per-worker hardware.

quiz.q: A vision team has a model that fits comfortably in the memory of one GPU, but its 4 TB image dataset takes days to train on one machine. Which approach is the best fit?
choices: Pipeline parallelism with the DeepSpeed distributor, because the model must be split across several GPUs
A larger driver for a single scikit-learn fit, since distributed training is always slower than one machine
Data parallelism with TorchDistributor, so each process holds the full model and reads its own data shard
Spark ML LogisticRegression on the image bytes, so that the table is processed in parallel across workers
quiz.explain: Because the model fits one device, replicas are possible and data parallelism divides the dataset among processes, which averages gradients to keep copies identical. Splitting the model, as DeepSpeed does, is for weights that do not fit. A single-machine fit does not finish in time for this much data, and Spark ML does not replace a vision network.

quiz.q: A cluster has 6 worker nodes, each with 48 cores and 4 GPUs. The team wants every Spark worker to host exactly one Ray worker that can use all of its cores and GPUs for Ray Tune. Which setup call does this?
choices: setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=24), so that each of the 4 GPUs of a node gets a separate Ray worker
setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=6, num_cpus_worker_node=48, num_gpus_worker_node=4)
setup_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=6, num_cpus_head_node=48, num_gpus_head_node=4), giving the head the hardware
setup_global_ray_cluster(max_worker_nodes=1), because a global cluster claims every GPU of the compute for itself
quiz.explain: The Databricks guidance is to set num_cpus_worker_node to the cores and num_gpus_worker_node to the GPUs of each Spark worker, so each worker launches one Ray worker that uses all of its resources. The head node mostly coordinates and defaults to no CPUs or GPUs, 24 workers would not match the hardware, and a global cluster concerns sharing, not sizing.

days.recap: Scale up before out, and distribute only when data or model exceed one machine. Use data parallelism when the model fits a device, DeepSpeed when it does not, Spark ML for classical algorithms on big tables, Ray for dynamic compute-heavy tasks, and size Ray workers to the hardware of each Spark worker.

days.title: Nested Runs, Custom Logging and Custom Models with Real-Time Feature Engineering

concepts.heading: Nested Runs for Searches and Cross-Validation
concepts.body: A tuning job or a cross-validation produces many pieces of work that belong to one candidate. MLflow models this with parent and child runs: starting a run with `nested=True` while another run is active creates a child linked to the active run, and the parent holds the summary, such as `cv_mean_auc`. Without `nested=True`, a second `start_run()` inside an active run raises an error, and ending the parent first would break the hierarchy. The legacy Hyperopt `SparkTrials` integration documents the same layout: the main run for the search and one child run per trial. The argument `nested=True`, the system tag `mlflow.parentRunId` and a `search_runs` filter such as `tags.mlflow.parentRunId = '<id>'` are standard MLflow behavior that no docs.databricks.com page spells out. Two traps follow. Parameters cannot be overwritten inside a run, so an autologged loop of fits needs one child run per fit. And the active run lives in the driver Python process, which executor code does not inherit automatically, so in `applyInPandas` return the metrics as rows and log child runs on the driver.

concepts.heading: Custom Metrics, Parameters, Tags and Artifacts
concepts.body: Choose the logging slot by data type. Metrics are numbers and can carry a `step`; parameters and tags are strings that `search_runs` can filter, with tags the usual home for labels such as a dataset snapshot date or a Git commit; artifacts are files. A runs table shows the latest value of a metric, so a curve logged per epoch ranks runs by the last epoch. Log a deliberate summary such as `best_val_loss` once at the end and sort by it. For in-memory objects, `mlflow.log_figure`, `mlflow.log_dict` and `mlflow.log_table` write an artifact without a temporary file (standard MLflow, not described on the Databricks pages). Autologging adds traps. On classic compute an interactive notebook calls `mlflow.autolog()` for you, but the docs say it is not applied to runs created with `mlflow.start_run()`, so you call `mlflow.autolog()` yourself; their example for adding custom logging to an autologged run uses `exclusive=False`. It is not enabled automatically on serverless compute, and it is active only on the driver node, so worker code must call `mlflow.autolog()` itself.

concepts.heading: Custom Model Objects with a pyfunc Wrapper
concepts.body: Built-in flavors log one library object. When a model is an XGBoost booster plus a fitted calibrator plus a business rule, wrap everything in a subclass of `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel`. Pass the fitted files through the `artifacts` argument of `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model`; the Databricks page on packaging artifacts shows them arriving in `context.artifacts` inside `load_context`, which runs once at load, while `predict(self, context, model_input)` runs per request. For plain scikit-learn preprocessing, fit one `Pipeline` (encoder, scaler, estimator) and log it as one model, so fitted statistics travel with the version. Learned preprocessing is part of the model: fit imputers and scalers on the training split only, because fitting before the split leaks held-out rows, and never recompute them on each scoring batch. A signature is required for models registered in Unity Catalog, and it should describe what callers actually send, which means raw columns, not engineered ones.

concepts.heading: Real-Time Feature Engineering Inside the Model
concepts.body: Request-time logic must exist once. If `make_features(df)` derives `days_since_signup` in training and a copy lives in the serving code, the two drift and predictions skew. Put the function in a module, import it in the training notebook and in `predict`, and ship it with the model through the `code_paths` argument of `log_model`. The private-libraries page spells it `code_paths` for a wheel, while the pyfunc and custom-models serving pages still show the older spelling `code_path` for shared modules and helper files; use `code_paths`. Then infer the signature from the raw input so clients send raw rows. When some inputs are stored features, log through the Feature Engineering client instead: `fe.log_model(model, artifact_path, flavor=mlflow.pyfunc, training_set=training_set)`. The lineage page documents this pyfunc flavor, and the model then records which feature tables and functions it needs, so Model Serving looks up keys and computes on-demand features before `predict` receives the assembled frame. A plain `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model` call records no feature dependencies.

examPoints: A hierarchical experiment, a search that writes one run per trial, or an error about an active run is testing `mlflow.start_run(nested=True)`, a summary metric on the parent and the best child found with `search_runs` on `tags.mlflow.parentRunId`.

Missing parameters or models after wrapping training in `start_run()`, on serverless compute, or inside `applyInPandas` points to the autologging limits: `exclusive=False`, an explicit `mlflow.autolog()` call, and logging from the driver.

A model with several fitted objects, rules or request-time feature code is a custom `PythonModel` with `artifacts`, `code_paths` and a raw-input signature; stored features that must be joined at serving time add `fe.log_model` with the training set.

quiz.q: A grouped-map job trains one model per store with `applyInPandas`. The notebook driver has an active parent run, and the function calls `mlflow.log_metric("rmse", e)`, but no per-store child runs appear. What is the most reliable fix?
choices: Call `mlflow.autolog(exclusive=False)` on the driver before the grouped call, so that every executor inherits the parent run and its tracking context
Pass `nested=True` to the `log_metric` call inside the function, so that the executor process attaches each metric to the parent run on the driver as a child
Return one row per store with its metric, collect the small result and log a nested child run for each store on the driver
Increase the number of shuffle partitions so that more executors share the driver's active run state while the grouped function is running
quiz.explain: The active run is state in the driver process, and executor Python workers do not inherit it automatically. Driver-side logging of the returned rows creates correct children. Autologging is enabled only on the driver, `log_metric` has no `nested` argument, and more partitions change task count, not run context.

quiz.q: A custom pyfunc's `predict` expects engineered columns `age_bucket` and `spend_ratio`, and its signature was inferred from the engineered training frame. Clients that send raw `age` and `spend` receive a schema error. Which change is correct?
choices: Build the features inside `predict`, share the helper through `code_paths`, and log with a signature inferred from raw input
Turn off signature enforcement on the endpoint, so that the missing engineered columns are ignored when the request reaches the model code
Ask every client team to reproduce the bucketing and the ratio exactly, because the signature has to describe the features used in training runs
Log the model again without any signature and add the engineered columns to every request payload through a default value in the endpoint settings
quiz.explain: The signature is the contract with callers, so it should list raw inputs, and the feature logic belongs inside the model version. Disabling validation does not create the columns, client-side engineering recreates skew, and removing the signature also blocks Unity Catalog registration.

days.recap: Nest one child run per trial, fold or fit under a parent that carries the summary metric, and log from the driver. Pick the logging slot by type, remember the autologging limits, and ship custom models as pyfunc wrappers that bundle fitted objects and shared feature code behind a raw-input signature.

days.title: Point-in-Time Correctness and Automated Feature Pipelines

concepts.heading: Why Plain Feature Tables Leak and How an As-Of Join Fixes It
concepts.body: A feature table that a nightly job overwrites keeps one row per entity, the newest. Joining twelve months of labels to it gives every old label today's feature values, some of which describe behavior after the label event. The model learns from the future, offline AUC looks excellent and production quality collapses. The fix is a time series feature table: a Unity Catalog Delta table whose primary key includes one `DATE` or `TIMESTAMP` column declared `TIMESERIES` (`timeseries_columns` in `FeatureEngineeringClient.create_table`, or `PRIMARY KEY (customer_id, ts TIMESERIES)` in SQL on Databricks Runtime 13.3 LTS or above). In `create_training_set`, a `FeatureLookup` names a `timestamp_lookup_key`, a column of the label DataFrame. For each label the join returns the latest feature row at or before that timestamp, or `null` if none exists. The docs state this is unrelated to Delta Lake time travel, which reads one snapshot of the whole table. A date key not declared as timeseries makes `create_training_set` and `publish_table` fail; change it to `STRING` only when exact matching is wanted.

concepts.heading: Behavior and Pitfalls of Point-in-Time Lookups
concepts.body: The lookup takes a whole row and keeps its nulls, so it does not fall back to an earlier non-null value. That is why a write to a time series feature table must supply values for all features, unlike partial merges into regular feature tables, and why a job writing only `temp` can mask an earlier `co2`. The optional `lookback_window` (a `datetime.timedelta`, default `None`) drops values older than the window during training and batch inference, but online inference always uses the latest value, so training and serving can disagree for dormant entities; add a feature that carries its own age if staleness matters. When you call `score_batch`, the DataFrame needs a timestamp column with the same name and data type as the training `timestamp_lookup_key`. Each `FeatureLookup` takes its own `timestamp_lookup_key`, but the docs show only one label timestamp column per training set. For speed, the docs recommend liquid clustering, `use_spark_native_join=True` on Photon, one timestamp key, no partition columns and at most two primary key columns.

concepts.heading: Creating and Converting Feature Tables
concepts.body: With `FeatureEngineeringClient`, `create_table` takes `primary_keys`, optional `timeseries_columns` and a DataFrame or schema, and `write_table` fills it, with `mode="merge"` updating rows by primary key, so a retried batch for the same `(store_id, hour_ts)` replaces rather than duplicates. An existing Delta table becomes a feature table in place: only the owner can declare the constraint, each key column is set `NOT NULL` first, then `ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT ... PRIMARY KEY (store_id, snap_ts TIMESERIES)`. A streaming table or materialized view from Lakeflow pipelines works the same way once its definition includes the key, though pipeline constraint support is Public Preview. A simple SELECT view over one feature-capable Delta table qualifies for offline training, with `databricks-feature-engineering` 0.7.0 or later, but it cannot be published to an online store, and joins or aggregations are outside that rule. Materialize an aggregate into a keyed table instead. Do not change the primary key, partition key, or name and type of an existing feature, which would break downstream pipelines.

concepts.heading: Automating the Feature Pipeline
concepts.body: A feature pipeline is ordinary code that computes a DataFrame and calls `write_table`. Schedule it as a Lakeflow Jobs task, keep the computation in a function that Git and tests cover, and have it merge by primary key so reruns are safe. To add features, update the computation and run `write_table`: the docs say this updates the schema and merges the new values. Streaming sources can feed the same table through a streaming `write_table`, which the docs support for time series tables too. At training time `create_training_set` joins the lookups and `load_df` returns the frame to train on; modifying that frame before training means the changes are not applied at inference. Log the model with `fe.log_model(..., training_set=training_set)` so `score_batch` and Model Serving repeat the lookups. For new projects the docs recommend Feature Views, where Databricks builds and runs the pipelines; hand-written feature tables remain the fit for Delta Sharing or third-party online stores, and this exam's tasks use the `FeatureEngineeringClient` table API.

examPoints: A large gap between offline and production quality with an overwritten feature table is leakage; the answer is a time series feature table with `TIMESERIES` in the key and `timestamp_lookup_key` in the `FeatureLookup`, not Delta time travel and not more cross-validation.

Nulls from a time series lookup, stale values online, or a `score_batch` error point to the row-as-a-unit rule (write all features), `lookback_window` applying only offline, and the matching timestamp column name and type in the scored DataFrame.

Converting an existing table means `NOT NULL` on key columns, then a primary key with `TIMESERIES`; views qualify only if they are simple SELECT views and never publish online, so joins and aggregations are materialized into a keyed Delta table.

quiz.q: `ml.sales.store_daily` has primary key `(store_id, snap_date DATE)`, created without the `TIMESERIES` keyword, and `create_training_set` now raises an error about the `DATE` key column. Each label must receive the latest snapshot on or before its own date. What is the fix?
choices: Cast `snap_date` to `STRING`, which keeps all the history and returns the most recent earlier snapshot for each label
Remove `snap_date` from the key and overwrite the table every night, so that each label joins to the one newest row
Upgrade `databricks-feature-engineering`, because newer releases treat any `DATE` key column as timeseries without any declaration at all
Declare `snap_date` as the `TIMESERIES` key and set `timestamp_lookup_key` in the `FeatureLookup` to the label date column
quiz.explain: As-of semantics come from the table key plus the lookup's timestamp column. A string key gives exact matching only, overwriting brings back leakage, and no client version infers the declaration.

quiz.q: A fraud model trained with `lookback_window=timedelta(days=7)` on a time series feature table returns 40-day-old values for dormant accounts from the online endpoint, while training saw `null`. What explains this, and what should the team do?
choices: The endpoint applies the window only when each request carries its own timestamp field, so add the transaction time to every request
Online inference always uses the latest value, so add an explicit staleness signal such as a last-updated feature
The online store keeps every historical row, so add the current date to the lookup key and send today's date with each request
The window takes effect online after the table is republished in `SNAPSHOT` mode, so schedule a nightly snapshot publish to apply it
quiz.explain: The docs say the lookback window applies to training and batch inference, while online inference always returns the latest value. The pipeline must therefore expose staleness itself. Request timestamps, date keys and publish modes do not change which stored value is returned.

days.recap: Point-in-time correctness comes from a time series feature table and a per-label as-of join, and its rules follow from that: whole rows with nulls, complete writes, offline-only lookback windows, matching timestamp columns at scoring. Build and convert tables with the Feature Engineering client, run merge writes from scheduled jobs, and log the model with its training set.

days.title: Online Feature Stores, Streaming Features and On-Demand Features

concepts.heading: Publishing to an Online Feature Store
concepts.body: Online Feature Stores replace the earlier online tables; they are powered by Lakebase and new stores are created as Lakebase Autoscaling projects. With the Feature Engineering client you call `fe.create_online_store(name=..., capacity=...)`, wait for the `AVAILABLE` state, then `fe.publish_table(online_store=store, source_table_name=..., online_table_name=...)`. The source needs a primary key with non-null columns, and the `TRIGGERED` and `CONTINUOUS` modes need Change Data Feed. `TRIGGERED` (the default) syncs increments on a schedule or API call; `CONTINUOUS` keeps a streaming pipeline running for immediate updates; `SNAPSHOT` copies everything once and is efficient when many existing rows change between syncs, for example a nightly recompute of most customers. For a time series table the online store holds only the latest row per entity, deduplicated during publish. Views cannot be published. Only one sync can run per online table at a time, so publish from a single final task or wait with `get_status()`; a second call is skipped with a message that the pipeline is already running.

concepts.heading: Operating Online Stores Safely
concepts.body: Serving endpoints look up an online table through its offline feature table, and with several online tables the docs say they always resolve to the oldest one, so publishing a second copy does not move traffic; version the feature table and create a new FeatureSpec and endpoint instead. Delete an online table with `WorkspaceClient().feature_store.delete_online_table(...)`, the only recommended method: a SQL `DROP TABLE` leaves the data in the database and the cost with it. Recreating a table, even with the same name, is a new Unity Catalog securable, so the endpoint's service principal loses its `SELECT` grant and lookups fail with `password authentication failed` while the endpoint still reports Ready; rebuilding means serving a changed model version or FeatureSpec so that permissions are set up again. For read-heavy latency problems add read replicas through `read_replica_count`, which also give availability; disabling high availability on a live store breaks connected endpoints, so build a new store, publish, point new endpoints at it, validate, then retire the old ones. Scale-to-zero is not supported.

concepts.heading: Computing Features from Streams
concepts.body: Real-time features follow one path: a Structured Streaming query turns events into feature rows, `write_table` accepts the streaming DataFrame and keeps the offline table current for training and lineage, and `publish_table` with `CONTINUOUS` pushes each change online where the logged model looks features up from keys. Event time belongs in the design. If late events upsert into a plain table, an old event can overwrite a newer one; a time series table keyed `(user_id, event_ts TIMESERIES)` turns each event into its own row and online publishing keeps the latest by timestamp. State must stay bounded: `withWatermark` plus `dropDuplicates` on an id and the event-time column removes replays, as the Spark guide describes, and deduplication belongs before the windowed count because an inflated aggregate cannot be repaired afterward. Windowed aggregates such as a ten-minute card count depend on history, so precompute them in the stream. The docs also describe Feature Views, which include streaming features and are recommended for new projects.

concepts.heading: On-Demand Features and Feature Serving
concepts.body: A value that depends on the request, such as `amount / avg_amount_30d` where the amount arrives only in the call, cannot be precomputed. Register a Python UDF in Unity Catalog, bind it with `FeatureFunction(udf_name=..., input_bindings=..., output_name=...)` next to the `FeatureLookup`s in `create_training_set`, and log with `fe.log_model(..., training_set=training_set)`. Then `score_batch` and Model Serving evaluate the same function, which removes training-serving skew. When a UDF input comes from a lookup that finds no key, it is `None` in `score_batch` but `float("nan")` online, so test both or set `default_values` on the lookup, which the docs introduce for IDs with no stored value. A UDF that imports packages needs `extra_pip_requirements`, in `fe.log_model` or in `create_feature_spec`. An application that wants feature values but no prediction deploys a `FeatureSpec` to a Feature Serving endpoint; the tables it references must be published online. To use a fresher value of a stored feature for one call, include it in the request payload and match the model's data type.

examPoints: A choice among `TRIGGERED`, `CONTINUOUS` and `SNAPSHOT` is decided by change pattern: small frequent changes need an incremental mode, immediate freshness needs `CONTINUOUS` with Change Data Feed, and mostly changed rows between syncs fit `SNAPSHOT`.

Cost that does not fall after `DROP TABLE`, an endpoint that ignores a new online table, or lookups failing after a table was recreated are the delete method, the oldest-table rule and the lost grant; high availability changes use a parallel store.

A feature that needs a value from the request is an on-demand Python UDF in Unity Catalog with `FeatureFunction`; handle `None` and `nan`, declare packages in `extra_pip_requirements`, and use Feature Serving with a `FeatureSpec` when no model is needed.

quiz.q: To cut cost, an engineer drops an unused online table with a SQL `DROP TABLE` and sees no savings on the Lakebase side. What is correct and what should be done?
choices: Call `WorkspaceClient().feature_store.delete_online_table(...)`; a SQL drop leaves the stored data in the database
Delete the source offline feature table, because an online table disappears when the table it was published from is removed
Set the store to scale to zero, which releases the data of unused online tables while the store itself stays available
Keep the SQL drop, since the storage pages are cleared after the next sync cycle and the savings then appear on the next invoice
quiz.explain: The docs name the SDK method as the only recommended deletion because it removes the table from Unity Catalog and from the database. Removing the source destroys training data, scale-to-zero is unsupported for online feature stores, and no sync cycle clears the leftover storage.

quiz.q: An on-demand UDF squares a value that comes from a `FeatureLookup`. Batch scoring works, but the online endpoint errors for brand-new users whose keys are not in the store. What is the likely cause and fix?
choices: Online serving accepts only UDFs written in SQL, so rewrite the function as a SQL expression and register it again
The online store rejects new users until `publish_table` is rerun in `SNAPSHOT` mode, so republish before the next request
A missing lookup is `None` in `score_batch` but `float("nan")` online, so handle both values or set `default_values`
Python UDFs cannot read lookup results, so send the stored value in the request payload as a raw input for every call
quiz.explain: The documented behavior is `None` in batch and `nan` online for unknown keys, so a function that tests only for `None` fails online. Python UDFs are the supported on-demand mechanism, snapshot republishing adds no keys, and UDFs can take lookup results as input bindings.

days.recap: Publish with the mode that matches the change pattern, publish from one place, delete with the SDK, and remember the oldest-table and grant rules when migrating. Stream features into the offline table with event time and bounded state, and compute request-dependent values with Unity Catalog UDFs shared by training, batch and serving.

days.title: Deploy-Code Lifecycle Pipelines and Mapping Databricks Features to Activities

concepts.heading: Deploy Code Versus Deploy Models
concepts.body: Databricks recommends promoting code, not models, in most situations. In deploy code, the training code moves from development to staging to production and trains the model in each environment: on a small subset in staging as an integration test, on full production data in production. Supporting code for features, inference and monitoring follows the same path through review and integration tests, retraining is safer because the code was approved, and models can be trained on production data that developers cannot read. In deploy models, the artifact trained in development is tested in staging and promoted. It fits when training is very expensive or hard to reproduce, all work happens in one workspace, or there is no external repository or CI/CD. Its costs are that supporting code needs a separate deployment path, which invites skew, that automated retraining is tricky, and that the pattern may not be viable when production data is not accessible from development. A hybrid trains in staging over full data and deploys that model to production. Environments usually map to catalogs: dev, staging and prod.

concepts.heading: The Pipelines That Move a Model Between Environments
concepts.body: The recommended architecture is a multitask job with training, validation and deployment tasks. Training evaluates on held-out data with the metrics chosen in development, logs to MLflow, registers a version in the catalog of the environment where the pipeline runs, and passes the model URI downstream with task values (`dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set`, then `.get(taskKey=..., key=...)`). Resolving the latest version instead can pick up another run's model. Validation loads that URI from Unity Catalog and checks format and metadata, selected data slices and compliance. A pass earns the `Challenger` alias; a failure records tags such as `model_validation_status`, annotations on the version, ends the run and notifies users. Deployment first compares `Challenger` with `Champion`, offline on held-out data tracked in MLflow or online by A/B test or gradual rollout, and moves `Champion` only if the challenger is at least as good. With no champion yet, use a business heuristic or threshold as baseline. Manual approval uses workflow notifications or CI/CD callbacks.

concepts.heading: From Pull Request to Production Jobs
concepts.body: Staging tests the pipeline code, not just the model. A pull request against the main branch builds the source and runs unit tests; a failure rejects the request. Integration tests then run all pipelines together (feature engineering, training, inference, monitoring), and for real-time use they create and test a serving endpoint in staging. To save time, tests may trade fidelity for speed with data subsets or fewer iterations. If everything passes, the code is merged, and creating a release branch triggers the CI/CD system to update production jobs. Databricks Git folders connect each workspace to the repository, so reviewed branches are the code that runs in each stage. Data scientists typically have no write or compute access in production, but read-only access to test results, logs, model artifacts and monitoring tables lets them diagnose problems and compare new models with the current one. Production inference reads the model by alias, so moving `Champion` changes what the next batch run loads without editing the inference job.

concepts.heading: Mapping Features to Lifecycle Activities
concepts.body: Match the activity to the feature that carries it. Recording how a version was built, with parameters, metrics, code snapshots and a link to the training data, is MLflow Tracking. Governed versions, per-environment permissions through catalogs and deployment status through aliases are Models in Unity Catalog, which replace stages. Ordering train, validate and deploy with dependencies, failure notifications and task values is Lakeflow Jobs. Code review and promotion between stages is Git with Git folders. Packaging feature lookups so callers send only keys is logging with the Feature Engineering client. Serving a version, updating an endpoint without downtime and splitting traffic for online comparison is Model Serving. Watching drift and quality of inputs and predictions is data profiling, formerly Lakehouse Monitoring. Retraining starts with scheduled jobs and moves to triggered retraining, where a SQL alert on a drift or quality metric calls a webhook that starts the training workflow. Tags record state but do not stop a pipeline, and traffic splits do not run offline evaluation.

examPoints: A scenario where supporting code diverged, production data is unreadable in development, or retraining must be trusted points to deploy code; deploy models is chosen for expensive training, a single workspace or no CI/CD.

Between pipeline tasks, the model URI travels in task values and never through a latest-version lookup; a version earns Challenger by passing validation, and Champion moves only after a comparison, against a baseline when none exists.

A mapping question is answered by the activity: tracking records lineage, Unity Catalog versions and aliases, Jobs orchestrate and notify, Git folders promote code, Model Serving serves and splits traffic, data profiling monitors.

quiz.q: Security policy blocks the development workspace from reading production data, so a team that promotes only trained models trains on synthetic samples in development. Which statement is correct, and what does Databricks recommend in most situations?
choices: Unity Catalog cannot register models from a development workspace, so the team must register each model from production after training
The pattern may not be viable without production data in development, so promote the training code instead
Synthetic samples are forbidden in every pattern, so copy the production data into development for training
The pattern forbids Git, so move exported notebooks by hand between the two workspaces after each approval
quiz.explain: The docs list inaccessible production data as a disadvantage of deploy models, and deploy code trains the final model in production on production data. Registration is not the limit, copying data breaks the policy, and Git is expected in both patterns.

quiz.q: A multitask job runs training, validation and deployment. Two runs can overlap, and validation must evaluate exactly the version that its own run's training task registered. How should the version reach the validation task?
choices: Training writes the model URI to a file under `/tmp` and validation reads that file from its own compute
Validation loads `models:/prod.ml.churn@champion`, because the alias always names the newest candidate
Validation calls `get_latest_versions` on the model name, because the highest number is always the current run's
Training sets a task value with the model URI, and validation reads it from the upstream task by task key
quiz.explain: A task value is scoped to the job run, so each validation task gets the URI its own training task produced. Local files are not shared between tasks, the champion alias points at the model already serving, and the highest version can belong to the other run.

days.recap: Promote code through dev, staging and prod, and let each environment train and test with its own catalog. Pass the model URI by task value, gate Challenger on validation and Champion on a comparison, and match each lifecycle activity to the feature that owns it.

days.title: Testing ML Code: Unit Tests, Integration Tests and Layout

concepts.heading: Unit Tests for Notebook Functions
concepts.body: A unit test checks one small function in isolation, early and often. Databricks shows the pattern with pytest. A function should return one predictable outcome of one data type: a column check returns true or false, a row count returns a non-negative whole number, never "false, or the thing itself". Run the tests against small fake DataFrames that copy the production schema, not against production tables, because a test must never change real data. By default pytest collects files named `test_*.py` (or `*_test.py`) and functions named `test_*`, so a file `checks_features.py` with `check_age_bucket` runs zero tests. Run the tests from a notebook, because the web terminal has no Spark support: `%pip install pytest`, then `retcode = pytest.main([".", "-v", "-p", "no:cacheprovider"])` after `sys.dont_write_bytecode = True` for read-only file systems. End with `assert retcode == 0`; without it a failing test leaves the job task green. The verbose results are in the cluster driver logs. Code kept in files outside notebooks must create its own Spark session, because only notebooks inject `spark`.

concepts.heading: Which Tests Run at Which Stage
concepts.body: In the Databricks MLOps workflow the stages split the tests. In development the team writes and runs unit tests while building the pipelines. In staging, CI starts on a pull request against main: it builds the code and runs the unit tests, and a failure rejects the pull request. Integration tests then run all the pipelines together (feature engineering, training, inference and monitoring), so a hand-off fault, such as a feature pipeline writing `cust_id` while training reads `customer_id`, fails here and not in production. When tests fail, the CI/CD system should notify users and post the results on the pull request; when they pass, the code merges to main and a release branch triggers the production update. The deployment pattern decides where the final tests run: with deploy code they run in staging, with deploy models only the artifact moves, so the final code tests run in development. Code tests do not validate a model: each newly trained production version still passes the validation pipeline before it gets the Challenger alias. Development can be given access to the staging catalog to debug a failure.

concepts.heading: Designing an Integration Test for the ML Pipeline
concepts.body: An integration test exercises the whole chain of feature computation, training, evaluation, deployment and inference, so every task must really execute. Keep staging as close to production as is reasonable, with the same libraries and cluster settings, and trade fidelity for speed or cost by shrinking the data or the training iterations, never by skipping steps. A nine-hour training run becomes a run on a small sample that still logs, registers and hands the model to inference. For real-time inference, trigger the model deployment pipeline so that it creates a temporary serving endpoint in staging, and send a few requests. In practice the test loads the model URI produced by the training task of the same run, passed along as a task value, not a released alias such as `@Champion`; otherwise the test passes while the new version is never touched. The docs also suggest scheduled integration tests on main when many pull requests merge concurrently. Giving each run its own schema in the staging catalog and dropping it afterwards, so parallel pull requests do not overwrite each other, is general engineering practice rather than a documented step.

concepts.heading: Organizing Functions and Their Tests
concepts.body: Databricks describes three layouts and recommends one per language. Functions and tests stored outside notebooks (files in a Git folder) can be imported by notebooks, job script tasks and external CI, and test frameworks such as pytest are designed to run there; the costs are more files to track, and the layout is not supported for Scala. Functions in one notebook and tests in another make reuse across notebooks easy, but the functions cannot be used or tested outside notebooks. Functions and tests in the same notebook are the simplest to maintain and the hardest to reuse, which suits a one-off analysis. The recommendation: for Python and R keep functions and tests outside notebooks; for Scala keep functions in one notebook and tests in a separate notebook; for SQL define the logic as SQL user-defined functions in a schema and call them, and their test queries, from SQL notebooks. Choose by reuse need: a wheel task or an external CI runner cannot import a function that lives only in a notebook.

examPoints: Test design: one predictable return type, fake data shaped like production, `test_*` names, `assert retcode == 0` so failures fail the task, results in the driver logs, Spark tests in a notebook.
Stages: unit tests on the pull request, integration tests across all pipelines in staging; final tests run in staging for deploy code and in development for deploy models.
Layout: Python and R outside notebooks, Scala as two notebooks, SQL as SQL UDFs in a schema; functions kept in notebooks cannot be reused outside notebooks.

quiz.q: A nightly job task runs `pytest.main([".", "-v"])` in a notebook. Last night two tests failed, yet the task shows success and the release continued. What change makes failing tests stop the pipeline?
choices: Install pytest with `%pip` in a separate first cell, because a missing installation lets the test run report success by default and hides failures
Run the same command in the web terminal of the cluster, whose process exit code fails the job task whenever any single test fails
Keep the return value of `pytest.main` and assert that it equals 0, so a failing run raises an error in the cell
Add `-p no:cacheprovider` to the call, because pytest otherwise swallows assertion errors that it has cached from earlier runs of the suite
quiz.explain: `pytest.main` returns an exit code instead of raising, so the cell succeeds unless the code is checked; asserting that it is 0 turns failing tests into a failing cell and task. Installing pytest, moving to the web terminal (which has no Spark support) or disabling the cache provider do not change how failures are reported.

quiz.q: Pull request integration tests must finish quickly, but training the full model takes many hours. The team still wants the test to catch hand-off faults between the pipelines. Which design fits best?
choices: Run all pipelines in staging on a small data sample or with fewer iterations, so training, registration and inference still execute
Skip the training task and load the released Champion model, because scoring is the only stage in which a hand-off fault can appear in practice
Run only the unit tests of the training function on the pull request, since they already cover the interfaces between all of the pipelines
Run the full training in the production catalog overnight, because only production-sized data can reveal a mismatch between column names
quiz.explain: Shrinking data or iterations keeps every step executing, so a broken interface still fails within the time budget. Loading the released model never touches the candidate, unit tests isolate single functions rather than interfaces, and testing in production risks real assets without being needed to find a name mismatch.

days.recap: Unit tests isolate single functions with fake data and fail the task through `assert retcode == 0`; integration tests run every pipeline together in staging, with less data but no skipped steps. Final tests sit in staging for deploy code and in development for deploy models. Python and R functions live outside notebooks, SQL logic in SQL UDFs.

days.title: Environments and ML Assets in Declarative Automation Bundles

concepts.heading: One Environment per Stage
concepts.body: Databricks recommends a separate environment for each stage, development, staging and production, with clearly defined transitions. An environment is compute, runtimes, libraries and jobs, and it usually corresponds to one Unity Catalog catalog (dev, staging, prod). Access follows roles. Data scientists have read-write access to dev and ideally read-only access to the prod catalog, including inference and metric tables, so they can diagnose quality and compare a new model with the live one. ML engineers own production, where data scientists normally have no write or compute access. If security forbids reading prod from dev, write a snapshot of production data into the dev catalog. Code, not models, moves between stages through Git: dev branch, main after staging tests, release branch for production. Production training can use a small configured set of top hyperparameters found in dev, which saves time and reduces run-to-run variance in automated retraining. Each environment registers models in its own catalog. Creating a registered model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`; adding a version needs ownership or `CREATE MODEL VERSION`.

concepts.heading: Standard Projects, Targets and Identities
concepts.body: Starting every project from the same layout is the job of the MLOps Stacks bundle template: `databricks bundle init mlops-stacks` asks whether to create `CICD_and_Project` (the default), `Project_Only` (ML code, for data scientists) or `CICD_Only` (infrastructure, for ML engineers). A bundle has targets such as dev and prod, chosen with `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`. A target with `mode: development` prefixes deployed resources with `[dev <user>]` and pauses schedules and triggers of jobs and quality monitors. A target with `mode: production` can check the Git branch, and Databricks recommends service principals for production deployments, set with `run_as`. Pitfall: when the deploying identity differs from the `run_as` identity, only jobs and pipelines are supported, so a bundle that also holds registered models or experiments should be deployed and run by the same service principal; `run_as` is not supported for model serving endpoints at all, and defining both in one bundle is an error. Values that differ per environment, such as the catalog, come from the target, for example `catalog_name: ${bundle.target}`, so promotion deploys the same reviewed code to another target.

concepts.heading: ML Assets as Bundle Resources
