concepts.body: The ML resource keys are `experiments`, `registered_models` and `model_serving_endpoints`, next to `jobs`; `models` is a legacy resource (Databricks recommends Unity Catalog `registered_models`) and `mlflow_experiments` does not exist. An experiment `name` must be an absolute workspace path, for example `/Workspace/Users/someone@example.com/my_experiment`, and a bare name fails. A registered model declares `catalog_name`, `schema_name` and `name`, plus `grants`, for example `EXECUTE` for a consuming group, which lets it load and call the model without changing it. A serving endpoint defines `config.served_entities` (`entity_name`, `entity_version`, workload settings) and a `traffic_config` with `routes`, each a `served_model_name` with a `traffic_percentage`. Two served entities routed 90 and 10 express a canary rollout inside one endpoint; the strategy is general practice, the fields are documented. `permissions` give an application `CAN_QUERY` without `CAN_MANAGE`. The `lifecycle` setting `prevent_destroy: true` stops a bundle from destroying a production registered model and its version history.

concepts.heading: Wiring Assets Together and Deploying
concepts.body: Assets in one bundle refer to each other through substitutions so that nothing is hard-coded. A training job that must log to the bundle's own experiment uses a reference of the form `${resources.experiments.<key>.id}` instead of a pasted ID, because the ID does not exist before deployment. The docs show this form for an app resource. One bundle can define the training job, the validation job, the registered model and the endpoint, so a pull request reviews pipelines and infrastructure together. A typical cycle is: `databricks bundle validate` flags unknown keys and wrong values, `databricks bundle deploy -t staging` creates the assets in the staging workspace and catalog, `databricks bundle run` starts the integration-test job, and CI repeats the deployment for prod from the release branch. Variables and targets let one YAML describe all three environments, each with its own workspace host, catalog and run identity. For fully automated workflows Databricks recommends OAuth machine-to-machine authentication with a service principal, not personal credentials.

examPoints: Environment = catalog plus workspace and jobs; data scientists get read-only access to prod (or a snapshot in dev); creating a registered model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`.

Bundle ML keys: `experiments` (absolute path name), `registered_models` (`grants`), `model_serving_endpoints` (`traffic_config` routes, `CAN_QUERY`); protect production assets with `lifecycle.prevent_destroy`.

Environment differences come from targets (`${bundle.target}`), `mode` and a service principal in `run_as`; different deployer and `run_as` identities support only jobs and pipelines, and `run_as` is unsupported with serving endpoints.

quiz.q: A bundle must send 10 percent of the requests of the endpoint `churn-ep` to a new model version while the current version keeps 90 percent. How is this declared?
choices: Create a second `model_serving_endpoints` entry for the new version and ask the application team to alternate calls between both endpoint names
List two served entities with distinct names in `config.served_entities` and set `traffic_config.routes` to 90 and 10 percent
Give the endpoint a `tags` entry such as `traffic: 10` on the new version, because the router weights requests by these tags
Set `route_optimized: true` on the endpoint, since route optimization splits the incoming requests between model versions by weight
quiz.explain: Served entities with distinct names and a `traffic_config` of routes give a weighted split inside one endpoint, and the split is reviewed with the bundle. Two endpoints leave the split to the callers, tags carry billing metadata and do not route, and route optimization concerns the request path, not the traffic weights.

quiz.q: A bundle declares a registered model, an experiment and a training job. The CI user deploys it with `run_as` set to a different service principal, and the deployment of the model and the experiment is rejected. What explains this?
choices: Bundles have no `experiments` resource type, so the experiment must be created by hand, and the registered model then fails with it
The CI user needs `CREATE MODEL VERSION` on the model, a privilege that bundles cannot grant, so every deployment of a model is rejected
A `mode: development` target blocks model creation by design, and the production target creates all of these assets in a later step
With different deploying and `run_as` identities only jobs and pipelines are supported, so deploy and run as the same service principal
quiz.explain: The run-as documentation limits a bundle to jobs and pipelines when the deploying identity and the `run_as` identity differ; using one service principal for both lifts that limit for registered models and experiments. Experiments are a documented resource type, and development mode pauses schedules instead of blocking creation.

days.recap: One catalog and workspace per stage, code promoted through Git, data scientists read-only on prod. Bundles describe `experiments`, `registered_models` and `model_serving_endpoints` with targets, `${bundle.target}` references, grants, permissions and `prevent_destroy`; deploy and run as the same service principal when registered models or experiments are involved (serving endpoints do not support `run_as`).

days.title: Automated Retraining and Selecting the Top Model

concepts.heading: Scheduled Versus Triggered Retraining
concepts.body: Databricks recommends beginning with scheduled, periodic retraining on the latest data and moving to triggered retraining when needed. A trigger is a signal from monitoring: a SQL alert on the drift or profile metrics tables, for example drift or model quality against a threshold, with a webhook destination that starts the training workflow. Alternatively a job can use a table update trigger on the metric table, so it starts when fresh rows land. The run-as principal needs `SELECT` on the monitored table, and with several tables the trigger fires when any or all of them update. Two options shape the timing: minimum time between triggers and wait after last change. The docs give an example: with 120 s and 60 s, updates at 5 s and 115 s do not start a run before 115 + 60 = 175 s, because the second update restarted the 60 s wait and the 120 s minimum had already passed. A table update trigger only says that new rows exist. The profile writes drift rows at every refresh, whether or not anything drifted, so the decision to retrain needs its own gate.

concepts.heading: The Retraining Job as a Pipeline
concepts.body: Build the job from tasks: check, train, validate, deploy. A check task counts the drifted columns in the drift metrics table and publishes the count with `dbutils.jobs.taskValues.set`. An `If/else condition` task evaluates `{{tasks.check_drift.values.drifted_columns}} > 0`, and only its true branch trains, so quiet nights cost one cheap task. The operators `>` and `<` compare numbers, while `==` and `!=` compare strings, so `12.0 == 12` is false. The train task hands the registered model URI to the validate task through a task value such as `{{tasks.train.values.model_uri}}`. Asking the registry for the highest version breaks when two runs overlap, because task values are scoped to the run. Use `Run if dependencies` for a task that must also run after a failure, for example a notification. Put a data-quality gate in front of training (general practice): drift cannot tell a change in behavior from an upstream defect, such as a feature set to null for part of the rows, and retraining on that data bakes the defect into the model.

concepts.heading: What a Retraining Trigger Can and Cannot Know
concepts.body: Drift is evidence that inputs changed, not that the model got worse, so it should start a challenger and not replace the champion. When labels arrive late, say about 45 days after scoring, daily feature or prediction drift gives the early start, and the labelled evaluation against the champion decides the promotion. After an abrupt and permanent change, such as a new regulation, keep volume by weighting or flagging the old regime instead of discarding all history, and measure on a holdout from the new period. When outcomes exist only for cases the model accepted, as with approved loans, every retrain grows more confident about the applicants it already liked, so exploration or reject inference is needed before the loop can be trusted. These points are general ML practice, not a Databricks page. The docs support the pattern drift or quality alert, then retraining job, then comparison, and note that a manual approval step can be added with workflow notifications or CI/CD callbacks when full automation is not wanted.

concepts.heading: Selecting the Top Model
concepts.body: Register every retrained model as a new version, give it the Challenger alias after the validation checks, and let consumers load `models:/<catalog>.<schema>.<model>@Champion`. The Champion alias moves only when the gate passes, and batch jobs and endpoints follow without code changes. Compare champion and challenger offline on the same fresh holdout, logging both in MLflow, never against a metric stored months ago. For real-time serving a longer online comparison, such as a gradual rollout or a traffic split between served models, is possible. Choose the metric to fit the problem; the rules from here on are general practice, not Databricks documentation. With 0.4% positives, a model that always predicts the majority class has accuracy 1 - 0.004 = 99.6%, so use PR AUC or recall at the precision the review team can afford. Use log loss and calibration when probabilities enter a formula, and a time-ordered split for time-dependent data. Require a margin plus a supported difference so the alias does not flip between near-identical models, rank runs on validation metrics and score the test set once, and treat latency and signature compatibility as pass or fail gates.

examPoints: Trigger design: scheduled first; a SQL alert with a webhook or a table update trigger gives the timing; an If/else task on a task value gates the decision; task values pass the model URI to validation.
A drift alert starts a challenger; evaluation on the same fresh holdout decides; Challenger alias first, Champion alias only after the gate, and consumers load the alias.

Metric choice follows cost (general practice, not documented): PR AUC or recall at precision for rare classes, log loss for probabilities, time-ordered splits, a margin for promotion, constraints as pass or fail gates.

quiz.q: A table update trigger on the drift metrics table starts the retraining job. The profile refreshes every night and writes rows each time, so a model is trained and registered every night even when nothing drifted. What is the best fix?
choices: Replace the trigger with a cron schedule on the training job, because only scheduled jobs can combine a drift check with training inside one run
Increase the wait after last change until the nightly profile rows no longer count as a table update for the trigger on that table
Grant the run-as principal fewer privileges on the metric table, so that only rows with detected drift are visible to the trigger
Add a first task that counts drifted columns and sets a task value, then an If/else task that trains only when the count exceeds zero
quiz.explain: The trigger only reports that rows were written, so the decision to retrain must come from a gate: a task value with the drift count feeds an If/else condition and the true branch trains. A schedule has the same problem, a longer wait only delays the run, and removing privileges would make the trigger fail to evaluate instead of filtering rows.

quiz.q: A fraud model has 0.4% positive transactions. The retraining pipeline picks the challenger with the highest validation accuracy, and last month's pick missed most fraud. Analysts can review a fixed number of alerts per day. Which selection metric fits?
choices: PR AUC, or recall at the precision that the review capacity allows
Mean squared error of the predicted label on the validation set, because it weighs all rows equally and is robust to the class balance
Training accuracy of the final model, because it shows how well the model has learned the rare class from the available examples
Accuracy on a validation set from which the rare class was removed, so that every remaining row is scored with the same weight
quiz.explain: With 0.4% positives a model that never flags fraud already has 1 - 0.004 = 99.6% accuracy, so accuracy hides the failure. PR AUC and recall at a fixed precision focus on the rare class and on the alert budget. The other options either still reward the majority class, measure the training set, or remove the class that matters.

days.recap: Start with scheduled retraining; move to alert-and-webhook or table update triggers with an If/else gate on a task value, and a data-quality check first. Drift starts a challenger, evaluation on the same fresh holdout decides, and the Champion alias moves only after the gate. Match the metric to the cost: PR AUC for rare classes, log loss for probabilities.

days.title: Drift Tests, Table Types and Monitor Features

concepts.heading: The Drift Metrics Table
concepts.body: Data profiling (the feature was called Lakehouse Monitoring before the rename) writes two metric tables beside the profiled table: `{table}_profile_metrics` and `{table}_drift_metrics`. The drift table compares windows and has one row per column, window, slice and drift type. `drift_type` is `CONSECUTIVE`, which compares a window with the previous one (`window_cmp`), or `BASELINE`, which compares it with the baseline table. Baseline drift exists only if a baseline table is given, and consecutive drift only if a previous window exists. Deltas are current minus comparison, for example `avg_delta`, `percent_null_delta` and `count_delta`. Slices appear as `slice_key` and `slice_value`, with NULL for the whole table, and `column_name` is `:table` for table-level metrics such as model accuracy. A test column holds NULL where the test does not apply to the type of the column. For an inference profile a good baseline is the data the model was trained or validated on. Alerts and dashboards read these Delta tables, so a drift rule is an ordinary SQL condition on them.

concepts.heading: Which Test for Which Column
concepts.body: The drift table computes different statistics by column type. Numeric columns get `ks_test` (a struct with statistic and pvalue), `wasserstein_distance` and `population_stability_index`. Categorical columns get `chi_squared_test` (statistic and pvalue), `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance` and `js_distance`. A NULL `ks_test` on a categorical column is therefore not a bug. The documentation states PSI bands: below 0.1 means no significant population change, below 0.2 moderate change, and 0.2 or more significant change. Example for four device types: baseline shares 40, 30, 20 and 10 percent, current shares 30, 20, 30 and 20 percent. Every absolute difference is 0.10, so `tv_distance` = 0.5 x (0.10 x 4) = 0.20, the share of traffic that moved to other categories, while `l_infinity_distance` is the largest single difference, 0.10. Wasserstein distance is measured in the units of the feature (standard definition, not stated on the page): if every basket value rises by 12 euros, it is 12, so analysts can set limits in euros.

concepts.heading: Reading Statistical Tests Correctly
concepts.body: A p-value measures how detectable a shift is, not how important it is. With hundreds of millions of rows per window, a rule such as `ks_test.pvalue < 0.05` fires daily on shifts too small to matter, so alert on an effect size instead: the KS statistic, Wasserstein distance or PSI, with thresholds taken from business impact. Multiple testing works against you too. Testing 300 numeric features at 0.05 gives 300 x 0.05 = 15 expected false alarms per refresh even when nothing changed. Correct for the number of tests (a Bonferroni level is 0.05 / 300, about 0.00017) or alert on effect size and feature importance. Small windows fail the other way: an hourly window with about 150 requests gives jumpy statistics, so use a coarser granularity so that each estimate rests on more rows. All of this is general statistics rather than a Databricks page, but the exam expects you to pick the metric whose wording matches the policy, such as share of traffic moved (`tv_distance`) or shift in euros (Wasserstein).

concepts.heading: Choosing the Table Type and the Monitor Feature
concepts.body: Pick the profile type from the table. Snapshot suits tables without a meaningful time axis or predictions, such as a customer dimension rewritten nightly: the whole table is profiled at each refresh, and very large tables go to time series. Time series needs a timestamp column and computes metrics per window, which fits large append-only event tables. Inference fits a request log with timestamp, model id, inputs, prediction and optional label, and adds quality metrics once prediction and label are both present. Then pick the feature. Baseline drift catches slow creep: a mean rising 0.3% a day moves 1.003^42, about 1.134 (+13.4%), in six weeks, yet every daily step is small. Consecutive drift catches sudden steps, and a spike followed by recovery shows as two consecutive alerts but only one differing window against the baseline. When inputs are stable but accuracy falls (concept drift), supply the label column. With delayed labels, watch prediction drift as a label-free early signal, and use slices to inspect segments.

examPoints: Drift table: `drift_type` CONSECUTIVE versus BASELINE; numeric columns use `ks_test`, `wasserstein_distance`, `population_stability_index`; categorical columns use `chi_squared_test`, `tv_distance`, `l_infinity_distance`, `js_distance`; NULL means not applicable.
PSI bands from the docs: below 0.1 no significant change, below 0.2 moderate, 0.2 or more significant; at large sample sizes alert on effect size, and correct for multiple tests (300 x 0.05 = 15).

Snapshot for tables without time axis, time series for timestamped event tables, inference for prediction logs; baseline drift for slow creep, consecutive for sudden steps, label column for concept drift.

quiz.q: The latest window of a numeric feature has `population_stability_index` = 0.15 against the baseline. How does the data profiling documentation classify this value?
choices: Moderate population change, because it is below 0.2, the value from which the change counts as significant
No significant change, because values stay acceptable up to 0.2 and only larger values count as population drift
Significant change, because every value of 0.1 or more is flagged and 0.2 is only the limit for a moderate change
Not applicable, because the index is calculated for categorical columns only and a numeric feature returns NULL there
quiz.explain: The documented bands are below 0.1 no significant change, below 0.2 moderate change and 0.2 or more significant change, so 0.15 is moderate. The index is calculated for numeric columns, and categorical columns are the ones that return NULL.

quiz.q: A categorical feature has four device types. Baseline shares are 40%, 30%, 20% and 10%; the current window has 30%, 20%, 30% and 20%. Product wants the rule "alert when at least 15 percent of traffic has moved to other categories". Which drift column and value apply?
choices: `l_infinity_distance` with a value of 0.10, which is below 0.15, so the rule does not fire for this window
`ks_test.statistic` with a value of 0.20, which categorical columns receive after their values are encoded as numbers
`tv_distance` with a value of 0.20, above the 0.15 limit
`wasserstein_distance` with a value of 0.20, which equals the share of traffic moved and therefore exceeds the limit
quiz.explain: Total variation distance is half the sum of absolute share differences, 0.5 x 0.40 = 0.20, which is exactly the share of traffic that moved, so it is above 0.15 and the rule fires. The L-infinity distance is only the largest single difference, and KS and Wasserstein are computed for numeric columns only.

days.recap: The drift metrics table separates CONSECUTIVE and BASELINE comparisons and fills KS, Wasserstein and PSI for numeric columns, chi-square, total variation, L-infinity and Jensen-Shannon for categorical ones. PSI 0.1 and 0.2 are the documented bands. Use effect sizes at scale, correct for many tests, and match profile type and drift comparison to the use case.

days.title: Building Monitors and Monitoring Pipeline Components

concepts.heading: Creating a Profile with the SDK
concepts.body: A profile (monitor) attaches to a Unity Catalog table. The creator needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` and `MANAGE`, and a table can have only one profile. Install a recent SDK with `%pip install "databricks-sdk>=0.68.0"` and call `w.data_quality.create_monitor(monitor=Monitor(object_type="table", object_id=table.table_id, data_profiling_config=config))`. The config holds `output_schema_id`, `assets_dir` and one profile type: `SnapshotConfig()`, `TimeSeriesConfig(timestamp_column, granularities)` or `InferenceLogConfig(problem_type, prediction_column, model_id_column, timestamp_column, granularities, label_column)`, where the label is optional. Optional parts are `slicing_exprs`, a cron `schedule`, `notification_settings` (for example emails when a refresh fails) and custom metrics. Refresh on demand with `create_refresh`; it runs on serverless compute, not on the cluster of the notebook. Granularities range from minutes to a year and set the window size. The older `quality_monitors` API is deprecated, so build new monitors with the data quality API. Deleting a profile does not delete its metric tables or dashboard.

concepts.heading: Behavior to Expect After Creation
concepts.body: Time series and inference profiles first analyze only a recent look-back, roughly the last month, and then process all new data. A profile created today on two years of history therefore shows about a month of windows, and no error is reported. Enable change data feed on the table so that each refresh processes only the newly appended rows. A profile on a materialized view does not support incremental processing, so refresh time grows with the view; unpack the data into a Delta table with change data feed instead. A snapshot profile reprocesses the whole table at every refresh and has a size cap, so a very large append-only table with a timestamp should use a time series profile, while a dimension table rewritten nightly suits snapshot. An inference profile with a prediction column but no label column still produces drift and distribution statistics, but accuracy, precision and recall stay NULL; model quality needs both prediction and label. For classification the quality metrics include `accuracy_score`, `f1_score` and `log_loss`; for regression `root_mean_squared_error` and `r2_score`.

concepts.heading: Monitoring an Endpoint Through the Inference Table
concepts.body: The pipeline for a served model has a fixed shape. Enable an inference table on the endpoint; AI Gateway-enabled inference tables are the current option and the older endpoint inference tables are retired. The table logs raw request and response JSON with status code and timing. A scheduled job unpacks the JSON into typed feature and prediction columns according to the schema of the endpoint, joins ground-truth labels when they arrive, and writes a flat Delta table with change data feed. The inference profile attaches to that flat table, not to the raw log, because it needs one row per request with a timestamp, a model id, the inputs and the prediction. Refreshing it fills the profile and drift metric tables and the dashboard. The roles differ: the raw inference table is for row-level debugging, such as the payload, status code and execution time of one complaint, while the profile tables hold aggregated trends. Do not change the schema or name of an inference table or delete it, because logging can stop.

concepts.heading: Components of a Monitoring Pipeline
concepts.body: A complete pipeline has five parts. Logging: the inference table records requests and responses. Drift: the drift metrics table, with consecutive and baseline comparisons. Performance: quality metrics in the profile metrics table once labels are joined. Health: endpoint health metrics for latency, request rate, error rate, CPU and memory, shown in the Serving UI for a limited period; for long retention, OpenTelemetry can persist logs, metrics and traces to Unity Catalog Delta tables that SQL can query. Action: Databricks SQL alerts on the metric tables with email, webhook or chat notifications, and a retraining job behind them. Access works as for any table: the profile creator owns the metric tables, so a risk team receives `SELECT` through ordinary Unity Catalog grants. One trap: profile refresh and dashboard refresh are separate. After the profile refreshes the metric tables, the dashboard shows old charts until it is refreshed too, and refreshing the dashboard does not recompute the profile.

examPoints: Build: `data_quality.create_monitor` with `SnapshotConfig`, `TimeSeriesConfig` or `InferenceLogConfig`; needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `SELECT` and `MANAGE`; one profile per table; label column required for quality metrics.
Large append-only tables: time series profile plus change data feed; materialized views are not processed incrementally; time series and inference profiles start with a recent look-back only.

Pipeline: inference table, unpack and label-join into a flat Delta table, inference profile, SQL alerts; row-level debugging uses the inference table, trends use the metric tables, and the dashboard refresh is separate.

quiz.q: An append-only table of clickstream events with an `event_ts` column keeps growing. A snapshot profile is rejected because the table is too large, and refresh cost must stay low. Which setup fits?
choices: A snapshot profile on a materialized view over the table, which is processed incrementally and so reads only the new events
A time series profile on `event_ts` with change data feed enabled on the table, so each refresh reads only new rows
An inference profile with `event_ts` as timestamp and the event type as prediction column, which supports tables of any size
A time series profile on a materialized view that unpacks the table, because views refresh faster than Delta tables
quiz.explain: A time series profile has no snapshot size cap and works by window on `event_ts`; change data feed lets each refresh process only appended rows. Materialized views are not processed incrementally by profiles, and an inference profile expects a prediction log, not clickstream events.

quiz.q: An inference profile refreshes on schedule and the drift tables fill normally, but accuracy, precision and recall are NULL in every window. The prediction column is configured. Which cause is most likely?
choices: The profile was created without a baseline table, which disables every accuracy-related column in the profile metrics table
Change data feed is disabled on the table, so the profile skips the quality computation and writes only the drift columns
The dashboard was not refreshed after the profile run, so the metric tables still hold the empty values from the first run
No label column with the ground truth is set, so quality metrics cannot be computed although drift statistics are
quiz.explain: Model quality needs prediction and label together; without the label column the profile still produces drift and distribution statistics. A missing baseline only removes baseline drift, change data feed affects cost and not which metrics exist, and the dashboard reads the metric tables rather than writing them.

days.recap: Create a profile with the SDK data quality API on a table you can manage: snapshot, time series or inference. Use time series plus change data feed for big append-only tables, flatten and label-join inference payloads before profiling, and remember the pipeline: inference table, drift, quality, endpoint health, alerts. Refresh the profile, then the dashboard.

days.title: Alerting on Drift, Choosing Baselines and Reading Performance Trends

concepts.heading: Drift Alerts Are Databricks SQL Alerts
concepts.body: Data profiling writes a profile metrics table and a drift metrics table, but it does not watch thresholds on its own. A profile alert is an ordinary Databricks SQL alert: you write a query on the profile or drift metrics table, create an alert on that query, set how often it is evaluated and choose where it notifies. Email is the default; a webhook, Slack or PagerDuty can also receive it. The profile's own notification settings are a different thing: they report refresh events such as a failed or timed-out refresh, never drift values. If the query has parameters, the alert runs with their default values, so a default model id or window silently pins the alert to the wrong version. For many features, one alert whose query returns every column over the threshold in the latest window is easier to own than one alert per column; this is general design practice, not a documented pattern. As general practice, add a freshness alert on the latest window end so a stalled profile cannot make the drift alert look quiet.

concepts.heading: Baseline Drift versus Consecutive Drift
concepts.body: The drift metrics table has a `drift_type` column with two values. `CONSECUTIVE` compares a window with the previous window and exists only when a consecutive window exists for the chosen granularities. `BASELINE` compares a window with the baseline table and exists only if a baseline table was provided, so a table with only consecutive rows means no baseline was configured. The baseline should match the schema of the profiled table, except the timestamp column, and for an inference profile it should also carry the same model id column. Good choices: training or validation data for an inference profile, a healthy copy for a snapshot profile, and a week, month or year of acceptable behavior for a time series profile. A baseline that is overwritten with the latest data after every retrain only measures drift since the last retrain and hides slow change. Numeric columns use statistics such as the population stability index (below 0.1 no significant change, 0.2 or above significant); categorical columns use distances and the chi-squared test. Delta columns are current window minus comparison window.

concepts.heading: Performance Trends from the Inference Workflow
concepts.body: Model quality needs predictions joined with ground truth over time. The documented workflow around inference tables is: log requests and responses, unpack the JSON payloads on a schedule according to the endpoint schema, optionally join the labels once they arrive, create an inference profile over the resulting Delta table and refresh it. Legacy endpoint inference tables are retired; Unity Gateway inference tables are the current feature, and their schemas differ, so unpacking code must match the one in use. To read a trend, query the profile metrics table with `column_name = ':table'`, `slice_key IS NULL` and the model id of interest, ordered by `window.start`. Slices per model id are created automatically, so two versions served in parallel can be compared. Accuracy, precision, recall and F1 need the label and prediction columns; log loss and ROC AUC also need `prediction_proba_col`; per-class F1 sits in the `one_vs_all` map of the `f1_score` struct. The inference table's `sampling_fraction` is 1 without down-sampling and below 1 with it, so carry it into the unpacked table: a plain count understates traffic, and the sum of `1 / sampling_fraction` estimates volume (our arithmetic, not a documented formula).

examPoints: Drift alerts are SQL alerts on the profile or drift metrics table; profile notification settings only cover refresh events and never check drift values.
No baseline table means no BASELINE rows in the drift metrics table; a baseline that is replaced by recent data after each retrain cannot show change since validation.
Quality trends: filter the metrics table on `:table`, `slice_key IS NULL` and a model id; log loss and ROC AUC need the probability column.

quiz.q: A team set email addresses in the profile's notification settings and expects a message when the population stability index of a feature passes 0.2. Drift is visible in the drift metrics table, but nobody is notified. What closes the gap?
choices: Raise the refresh frequency of the profile so that the notification settings re-check the drift values after every window
Enable the baseline table option in the notification settings so drift rows are compared with a threshold
Create a Databricks SQL query on the drift metrics table and an alert on it that sends to the team's chat destination
Add the address to the endpoint's permissions so that rows of the drift metrics table are mailed on arrival
quiz.explain: Notification settings of a profile report events such as a failed or timed-out refresh and never evaluate drift values. A drift threshold needs a query on the drift metrics table with a SQL alert and a notification destination. A faster refresh only produces data sooner, a baseline table is not a notification option, and endpoint permissions do not send mail.

quiz.q: The drift metrics table of a time series profile contains only rows with `drift_type = 'CONSECUTIVE'`, yet the team wants to compare current traffic with the data the model was validated on. What is missing?
choices: A baseline table holding the validation data, set in the profile configuration with a matching schema
A second granularity, because baseline rows appear only when the profile uses two granularities
A custom drift metric, since the built-in drift table never contains comparisons with reference data
A larger slicing expression list, because slices are what create comparison rows against the training set
quiz.explain: Baseline drift is calculated only if a baseline table is provided, so a table with only consecutive rows means none was set. Granularities decide the windows and slices decide subsets; neither creates a reference comparison. The built-in drift table does hold baseline rows once a baseline exists, so no custom metric is needed.

days.recap: Drift alerting is a SQL alert on the drift table plus a freshness alert; baseline drift needs a baseline table with the profiled schema that does not move with the data; quality trends come from the `:table` rows of the inference profile, per model id, with the probability column for log loss and ROC AUC.

days.title: Custom Metrics, Granularity, Slicing and Endpoint Health Metrics

concepts.heading: Aggregate, Derived and Drift Custom Metrics
concepts.body: Custom metrics extend the built-in statistics and come in three kinds. An aggregate metric reads the profiled table and is stored in the profile metrics table, for example the share of rows whose absolute prediction error exceeds a limit. A derived metric is computed from aggregate values that already exist, such as the square root of a stored squared average, so it needs no new scan of the table. A drift metric compares an aggregate or derived metric across two windows, written with `{{current_df}}` and `{{base_df}}`, and is stored in the drift metrics table. The `definition` is one SQL expression written as a Jinja template; it cannot contain joins or subqueries, so a value from another table must first become a column of the monitored table or of a view. Use `input_columns=[":table"]` for a metric that uses several columns, and the `{{prediction_col}}` and `{{label_col}}` parameters only in inference profiles; in other profile types name the real columns. A metric with `input_columns=["f1", "f2"]` appears on the rows of those columns, and a `:table` metric on the `:table` row.

concepts.heading: Granularity and Slicing Change the Row Count
concepts.body: Every metric is computed for each combination of window, slice and, for inference profiles, model id. Granularities (five minutes up to one year) set the window length; with two granularities the metric tables hold rows for both, so a chart or a sum must first filter the `granularity` column. The whole table is the slice with `slice_key IS NULL`; each entry of `slicing_exprs` adds slices next to it, so summing counts without filtering `slice_key` multiplies the total. A slice is defined by a single key, which means a combination such as region and device needs one expression or one column that combines them. A Boolean expression such as `amount > 1000` gives one key with the values true and false, read with `slice_key = 'amount > 1000' AND slice_value = 'true'`. For classification, Boolean slices also receive fairness and bias statistics. A column with millions of distinct values would create one slice per value (our reasoning from that rule); slice on bounded segments or buckets and find single users with a query on the inference table.

concepts.heading: Reading Endpoint Health Metrics
concepts.body: Endpoint health metrics describe the serving infrastructure, not the model's quality: latency, request rate, request error rate (4xx and 5xx together), CPU usage, memory usage, request queue time and model inference latency. The Metrics tab shows the last 14 days, and `/api/2.0/serving-endpoints/<name>/metrics` can be scraped by Prometheus over https with a bearer token; Datadog has an integration. The latency chart is the round trip inside Databricks, so a client also sees authentication and rate limiting. Read the metrics as a set: high queue time with low model inference latency and high CPU means the endpoint is under-provisioned, so widen the compute scale-out range. Doubled inference latency with an idle queue means the time is spent in the model call, which includes feature lookups, so more replicas will not help. Memory that climbs while the request rate is flat suggests a leak (general diagnosis, like the inference-latency reading). To split the error rate into client and server faults, group the inference table by `status_code`; raising `MlflowException` in model code maps to 4xx.

examPoints: Aggregate metrics scan the table, derived metrics reuse stored aggregates, drift metrics compare two windows; definitions have no joins or subqueries.
Filter `slice_key IS NULL` for totals and the `granularity` column before charting; one slice key per slice, so combine columns first.
Queue time high and inference latency flat means add capacity; inference latency high and queue idle means fix the model call; the error split comes from `status_code`.

quiz.q: A team wants a metric that multiplies each row's churn probability by a margin stored in a separate dimension table. A custom metric definition with a join is rejected. What is the supported design?
choices: Register the join as a derived metric, so that the lookup runs against the stored aggregate values only
Make the margin a column of the monitored table or a view, then use an aggregate metric
Move the expression into a drift metric, because drift definitions are allowed to contain subqueries
Put the dimension table into the baseline table, which lets every metric read it directly at refresh
quiz.explain: A definition is a single SQL expression without joins or subqueries, so the value must become a column of the monitored table or a view that contains it, and the metric is then an aggregate over the raw columns. A derived metric only uses stored aggregates, drift definitions have the same restriction, and a baseline table is a reference for drift, not a lookup source.

quiz.q: During the daily peak a custom endpoint answers slowly. Total latency P99 and request queue time P99 climb, model inference latency P99 stays low and CPU is high on every replica. What is the best action?
choices: Compare the new model code with the previous version for slower feature lookups
Move the clients to the inference table and read predictions from there instead of querying
Add an alert on the error rate, since 4xx responses are the cause of queued requests
Widen the compute scale-out range so that more requests are processed in parallel
quiz.explain: High queue time with flat model inference latency and saturated CPU shows that requests wait for a free replica, which is a capacity problem, so more scale-out helps. Slow code or lookups would raise the inference latency instead, an inference table is a log and not a serving path, and an error alert measures failures, not waiting time.

days.recap: Pick the metric type by what it reads (table, stored aggregates or two windows), filter `slice_key` and `granularity` before summing, and diagnose an endpoint by comparing queue time, model inference latency, CPU and memory before changing capacity or code.

days.title: Deployment Strategies and Rollouts with Model Serving

concepts.heading: Canary, Blue-Green and Shadow Compared
concepts.body: These strategies are general release practice, not Databricks features with their own documentation page; on Databricks you build them from served entities, traffic routes and endpoints. A canary sends a small share of live requests to the new version and raises it in steps while error rate, latency and a quality signal stay healthy. It fits high-traffic applications because even a few percent gives enough requests to judge, and it limits the damage of a bad version. Blue-green prepares a complete second environment, tests it and switches all callers at once, keeping the old one for rollback; it fits a change that cannot run next to the old version, for example a new required input column, but it pays for two environments until the old one is retired. A shadow run copies each request to the candidate whose answers no caller sees; `traffic_config` only splits traffic, so the copy comes from the client or a replay job. At low traffic a canary yields too few requests to prove anything, so replay recorded requests against the new version and then switch.

concepts.heading: Implementing a Canary with Served Entities
concepts.body: One endpoint can serve several models: each served entity has a name such as `current` or `challenger`, and `traffic_config` lists routes with `served_model_name` and `traffic_percentage`. The documented example splits 90 and 10, and the split is changed by submitting an updated configuration. A single served entity can still be queried directly at `/serving-endpoints/<endpoint>/served-models/<name>/invocations`, and the traffic settings are then ignored, which allows tests without exposing users. Until a new configuration is ready the old one keeps serving, only one update can run at a time, and an update that is under way can be cancelled from the endpoint page; if an update fails, the active configuration stays effective, so a pipeline must poll the endpoint state instead of trusting the call that returned. Roll back by one update that gives `current` all the traffic and removes `challenger`. Size each served entity from its own share, because concurrency is roughly requests per second times run time, and avoid scale to zero for a canary, since a cold start distorts its latency.

concepts.heading: Blue-Green and Route Optimization with Two Endpoints
concepts.body: A blue-green rollout uses two endpoints, so the switch happens in the client or gateway that holds the endpoint name, not inside one traffic split. Permissions are set per endpoint, and the identity that will call green, often a service principal, needs query access on it; validating with that identity before cutover catches a 403 early. The recorded creator of an endpoint needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `EXECUTE` on the model, and updates re-check it, so a long-lived service principal is the safer creator. Route optimization can be enabled only when an endpoint is created, never on an existing one, so moving a busy endpoint to it is also a blue-green move: create a new route-optimized endpoint for the same model version, test it at its own URL with an OAuth token that carries `authorization_details`, move clients and keep the old endpoint. Keep blue until the labeled results of the new version are checked, which may take days.

examPoints: Canary raises a share on live traffic and needs enough requests; blue-green switches a whole second environment and suits breaking input changes; both have no docs page.
Splits live in `traffic_config` routes of served entities; one update at a time, the old configuration serves until the new one is ready, and rollback is one update.
Permissions are per endpoint, route optimization is chosen at creation only, and the old environment stays until the new version is verified.

quiz.q: A recommendation model is retrained and will serve a sustained 2,000 requests per second. Offline tests look good, but the team fears subtle quality regressions in production. Which rollout fits best?
choices: Blue-green with a full second endpoint and one cutover for all users once the offline tests pass
Canary at a small share, watching errors, latency and quality, then raising the share in steps
Shadow evaluation for one hour and then deleting the old served entity to save the compute cost
A scale-to-zero challenger that receives live traffic only at the moments when the current model is idle
quiz.explain: With high traffic a small canary share yields enough requests to compare error rate, latency and quality while limiting the effect of a regression, and the share rises as evidence grows. A single blue-green cutover exposes all users at once, deleting the old entity removes the rollback path, and a scale-to-zero entity would add cold-start latency that distorts the comparison.

quiz.q: An endpoint serves `current` at 80 percent and `challenger` at 20 percent. The challenger's error rate climbs while `current` is healthy. The team wants users off the challenger quickly without an outage. What should it do?
choices: Submit one update that gives `current` all traffic and removes `challenger`
Delete the endpoint and create it again with only `current`, because routes of a live endpoint cannot be edited
Submit separate updates in parallel, one for the percentages and one for removing the entity
Set the challenger's workload size to zero so that its routes stop receiving any requests
quiz.explain: A configuration update can change the routes and remove the entity at once, and the old configuration serves until the new one is ready, so there is no outage. Deleting the endpoint causes downtime, only one update can run at a time so parallel updates fail, and a workload size is a compute setting, not a way to stop routing.

days.recap: Choose canary for subtle regressions on enough traffic and blue-green for breaking changes or a clean rollback; implement a canary with named served entities and `traffic_config`, change it with a single update, and keep the old version until its results are verified.

days.title: Custom PyFunc Models, Querying and Deploying with the Deployments SDK

concepts.heading: Packaging a Custom PyFunc Model
concepts.body: A custom PyFunc model wraps preprocessing, postprocessing or an unsupported framework in a class with two methods. `load_context` runs once and holds everything expensive: read weights, build tokenizers. `predict` holds the per-request logic only, so loading a file inside it makes every call slow. Files the model needs at serving time must be packaged with the `artifacts` argument of `log_model`; the documented reason is that Model Serving requires Unity Catalog volume files to be packaged into the model, and the code then reads them from `context.artifacts`. A tokenizer fetched from the internet at load time breaks when network access is blocked, so download it when logging and load it with `local_files_only=True`. Shared code folders use `code_path` on the PyFunc page (the private-libraries page writes `code_paths`; never hinge an answer on the spelling). Registration in Unity Catalog requires a model signature, which an `input_example` or `infer_signature` provides. On Databricks Runtime ML, name `mlflow` in `pip_requirements`, because the default `mlflow-skinny` stops the container build.

concepts.heading: Querying an Endpoint: REST and Deployments SDK
concepts.body: Custom model endpoints accept pandas DataFrame JSON as `dataframe_split` (recommended) or `dataframe_records`, and tensor input as `instances` or `inputs`. The records format does not guarantee column order, so a model that reads columns by position can return different results than in the notebook; send the split format with explicit columns and select columns by name. The response wraps results in a `predictions` key. From Python the MLflow Deployments SDK `predict()` queries the endpoint; any other client posts JSON to `/serving-endpoints/<name>/invocations`; `ai_query` is the SQL option. Databricks recommends machine-to-machine OAuth tokens for production. A route-optimized endpoint is different: it accepts only OAuth tokens, must be queried at its dedicated URL, and the token needs `authorization_details` that name the endpoint and the `query_inference_endpoint` action, otherwise the call returns 401. Protobuf tensor input is Public Preview, so JSON stays the answer. Input errors raised as `MlflowException` return 4xx, so malformed requests do not look like platform faults.

concepts.heading: Deploying and Debugging a Custom Model Endpoint
concepts.body: Create the endpoint with the Deployments SDK client (from `mlflow.deployments.get_deploy_client("databricks")`), the REST API or the UI, giving each served entity the model name, version, workload size and scale-out. Endpoint names cannot start with `databricks-`, which is reserved. The recorded creator needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `EXECUTE` on the model, checked at creation and update. Dependencies come from the model's requirements: a private mirror configured as the workspace default repository is used during the build, and an internal wheel is passed through `extra_pip_requirements`. A missing module at startup means a new model version with the dependency, then an endpoint update. Keys belong in a Databricks secret, referenced as `{{secrets/scope/key}}` in the served entity's environment variables; the creator needs READ on the secret. Before deploying, `mlflow.models.predict` with an input example tests predictions in a virtual environment that simulates serving; for a failing `predict()`, load the model in a notebook. Express deployments shorten builds and keep the environment equal to training, at the cost of seconds to a minute more at registration. A 429 about concurrency means raising scale-out toward QPS times run time.

examPoints: `load_context` loads once, `predict` runs per request; package files with `artifacts`, a signature is required in Unity Catalog, and `mlflow` (not `mlflow-skinny`) goes into `pip_requirements`.
Send `dataframe_split` with explicit columns; route-optimized endpoints need OAuth tokens with `authorization_details` and their own URL.
Endpoint names cannot start with `databricks-`; creator grants are `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA`, `EXECUTE`; secrets use `{{secrets/scope/key}}`.

quiz.q: A pyfunc model loads its weights with `torch.load("/Volumes/ml/prod/weights/model.pt")` inside `predict`. It works in a notebook but is slow and fails when served. Which change fixes both problems?
choices: Log the file with `artifacts` and read it once in `load_context`
Copy the volume path into an environment variable and keep loading the file inside `predict`
Register the model without a signature so that Unity Catalog skips the file check on registration
Wrap `torch.load` in a retry loop inside `predict` until the volume is mounted for the endpoint
quiz.explain: Model Serving needs the files packaged into the model with the artifacts argument, and loading once in the context method keeps per-request work small. An environment variable still points to a path the endpoint cannot read, a missing signature breaks Unity Catalog registration, and retries inside the request path only add latency.

quiz.q: A service principal queries a route-optimized endpoint at its dedicated URL with a token minted using `scope=all-apis` only. Every call returns 401. What must change?
choices: Switch to a personal access token, because route-optimized endpoints accept only those tokens
Send the request to the workspace invocation URL, which every endpoint keeps after creation
Grant the principal EXECUTE on the model, which unblocks the authentication of its requests
Mint the token with `authorization_details` for the endpoint and its query action
quiz.explain: A route-optimized endpoint needs an endpoint-scoped OAuth token, so the token request must carry authorization details with the query action. Personal access tokens are not supported there, the workspace URL does not apply to such endpoints, and EXECUTE on the model is an endpoint creation grant, not a query authentication fix.

days.recap: Package files and dependencies at logging time, load once in `load_context`, send column-safe requests, use endpoint-scoped OAuth for route optimization, and fix deploy failures by logging a new model version and updating the endpoint.

days.title: Final Review: Decision Cheat-Sheet Across the Three Domains

concepts.heading: Domain 1, Model Development (44 percent)
concepts.body: Choose the engine first. Spark ML fits data that does not fit one machine, with pipelines of estimators and transformers; single-node libraries fit data that fits in memory, and a trained single-node model can be scored in parallel with a pandas function or a UDF. For tuning, teach Optuna with the MLflow storage or Ray; open-source Hyperopt is unmaintained and is only a legacy comparison, and `xgboost.spark` is Public Preview, so it is not the answer. Parallelism: data parallelism splits the data across workers, model parallelism splits one model, and a vertical upgrade fits a task that is limited by one machine. In MLflow, nested runs group a tuning parent with child trials. Features: Unity Catalog feature tables with point-in-time joins on timeseries keys prevent leakage; Online Feature Stores (formerly online tables, Lakebase-backed) serve low-latency lookups; on-demand features are Python functions registered in Unity Catalog that compute at request time. The workspace Feature Store is deprecated.

concepts.heading: Domain 2, MLOps (44 percent)
concepts.body: Prefer deploy code over deploy models unless training is expensive, there is one workspace or there is no CI/CD: the training code is promoted through environments and retrains on production data, and aliases such as `Champion` replace stages. Test at two levels, unit tests for functions and integration tests that run the pipeline per environment, and keep functions in importable modules. Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles) define experiments, registered models and serving endpoints as code. Retraining is triggered by schedule, by new data or by a monitor signal, and a challenger is judged on the same fresh holdout, with the Champion alias moving only after the gate. Monitoring: pick the profile type by the question, snapshot for a table's state, time series for windows over time, inference for models with predictions and labels. Data profiling (formerly Lakehouse Monitoring) writes metric and drift tables; the PSI bands are 0.1 and 0.2; alerts are Databricks SQL alerts. Use a baseline for change since validation, consecutive windows for change since the previous window, custom metrics for business rules, and slices for subgroups.

concepts.heading: Domain 3, Model Deployment (12 percent) and Exam Tactics
concepts.body: Deployment questions test strategy and mechanics. Canary suits subtle regressions on high traffic and blue-green suits breaking input changes or an instant rollback; both are implemented with served entities and `traffic_config` or with two endpoints, and neither has its own docs page. One update runs at a time, and the old configuration serves until the new one is ready. Custom pyfunc models load heavy objects once, package files with `artifacts`, need a signature in Unity Catalog, and are queried with `dataframe_split` through the Deployments SDK `predict()` or REST; route-optimized endpoints need endpoint-scoped OAuth. Creating a registered model needs `USE CATALOG`, `USE SCHEMA` and `CREATE MODEL`; adding a version needs ownership or `CREATE MODEL VERSION`. Endpoint inference tables are legacy; Unity Gateway inference tables are current. The exam has 59 scored questions in 120 minutes and a pass mark that is not published. Weight your time 44, 44 and 12 percent, eliminate options that rely on Preview features or hand-written code for what the platform does, and read the stem for the decision being asked.

examPoints: Weights: D1 Model Development 44 percent, D2 MLOps 44 percent, D3 Model Deployment 12 percent; 59 scored questions in 120 minutes, pass mark unpublished.

Pick the design the stem asks for: Spark ML vs single node, Optuna vs Ray, deploy code vs deploy models, snapshot vs time series vs inference profile, baseline vs consecutive drift, canary vs blue-green.
Treat Hyperopt, `xgboost.spark`, protobuf tensor input and legacy inference tables as distractors, and use the current names: data profiling, Online Feature Stores, Declarative Automation Bundles.

quiz.q: A team must choose how to learn about slow quality decay of a deployed classifier whose labels arrive a week late. Which design uses the platform instead of custom code?
choices: A notebook that reads dashboard widgets every hour and posts a message to the team by webhook, written and run by the team
An inference profile with label and prediction columns, plus a SQL alert on its metrics
A canary that sends all traffic to the new model and compares only the first hour of results
A snapshot profile on the model registry table, refreshed after every single request that the endpoint serves
quiz.explain: An inference profile computes quality metrics per window and model id once labels are joined, and a SQL alert on the metric tables notifies the team without custom polling code. Reading dashboard widgets replaces a built-in mechanism, a canary is a rollout tool and not a monitor, and a snapshot of a registry table says nothing about predictions.

quiz.q: A retailer will serve a retrained model whose new required input column breaks the old version. Which statement describes the right rollout and its cost?
choices: Canary at 5 percent on the same endpoint, because both versions accept the same kind of requests
Replace the served entity in place during the daily peak so that no second environment is paid for at all
Blue-green on a new endpoint: clients switch at cutover and two endpoints are paid for until the old one retires

quiz.explain: A new required input column means the old version rejects the new requests, so both versions cannot share one split; a separate endpoint is tested first, clients switch at cutover and the old endpoint stays for rollback, at the cost of two environments for a while. A canary would send incompatible requests to one version, an in-place replacement removes the rollback path, and shadow evaluation by definition hides the new answers.
